items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place, pointing at yourself to introduce who you are. You want to say "I'm a student." You've got the words — 私[わたし] for *I*, 学[がく]生[せい] for *student* — but how do you glue them together so it sounds like a real sentence and not two nouns dropped on the floor? That glue is は, the topic marker.

は is the very first particle most learners meet, and for good reason: it's how Japanese says "okay, here's what I'm talking about — now let me tell you something about it." You name your topic, stick は after it, and then make your comment.

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]です。
```

*I'm a student.*

That's the whole shape. 私[わたし] is the topic, は marks it, and 学[がく]生[せい]です is the comment about it. Notice one thing right away that trips everyone up the first week: this particle is written with the character は but pronounced *wa*, not *ha*. That's normal — it's a historical spelling quirk, and it only happens when は is doing this topic job.

## How it works

The structure is simple: **Noun + は + comment**. The noun is what you want to talk about. は announces it as the topic. Everything after は is your statement about that topic.

Think of は as drawing a line: "As for this thing — here's the deal." A loose but useful translation of は is "as for." *As for me, student.* Clunky in English, perfectly natural in Japanese.

```jp
これは本[ほん]です。
```

*This is a book.*

Here これ (this one) is the topic, and 本[ほん]です (is a book) is the comment. The comment doesn't have to be short, and it doesn't have to be a です sentence either — but everything you know so far ends in です, so that's what we'll lean on.

You can make the topic a person's name, a pronoun, or any noun at all:

```jp
彼[かれ]は学[がく]生[せい]です。
```

*He is a student.*

```jp
あなたは学[がく]生[せい]です。
```

*You are a student.*

The pattern never changes based on what the topic is. は itself doesn't conjugate, doesn't shift form, doesn't care whether the topic is singular or plural. It's one of the most stable pieces of machinery in the whole language — it just sits there marking the topic, every single time.

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest thing to internalize: は marks the **topic**, not necessarily the grammatical subject. In simple sentences these overlap so much that you won't feel the difference yet, but keep the word "topic" in your head. It'll matter soon.

Because は sets up "what we're talking about," Japanese loves to drop things once the topic is clear. If it's obvious you're talking about yourself, you can leave off 私[わたし]は entirely and just say 学[がく]生[せい]です. That's not lazy — it's how the language breathes. The topic, once established, doesn't need repeating.

> は is pronounced *wa* when it's the topic marker, even though it's written with the character for *ha*. When は is just part of a word (not a particle), it's read *ha* normally. This one spelling quirk confuses everyone at first — you're not misreading it.

One more caution: don't sprinkle は onto every noun in a sentence. A sentence usually has **one** topic. Marking two different nouns with は in the same breath will sound strange unless you're deliberately drawing a contrast, which is a move you'll learn later.

## Casual speech

Good news here: は as a topic marker stays は in casual speech. It doesn't contract or drop the way some particles do. What changes around it is the *comment* — casual speakers often drop the です at the end.

```jp
これは本[ほん]。
```

*This is a book. (casual)*

Same topic, same は, just a more relaxed comment with です chopped off. So the particle you're learning now carries straight over into casual speech unchanged — one less thing to relearn later.

## Contrast

You haven't met other particles yet, so there's nothing to line は up against just now. But here's the tease worth holding onto.

Very soon you'll meet が, the subject marker. It looks like it does the same job as は — and the difference between は and が is one of the genuinely hard, genuinely famous puzzles in Japanese. The short version: は says "as for X, here's the news," while が points a spotlight and says "*X* is the one." You don't need that distinction yet, but plant a flag here, because when が arrives, the first question will be "wait, how is this different from は?"

You'll also soon meet を for marking the object of a verb, and の for linking nouns together. All three live in the same neighborhood as は — little particles doing the quiet structural work — but は is the one that sets the stage for everything else.

Recap: name your topic, add は (say it *wa*), then comment. That's the backbone of the Japanese sentence, and you'll use it in nearly everything you ever say.
caution_notes: は as a topic marker is pronounced wa, not ha, even though it's written with the ha character.
は marks the topic (what you're talking about), which is not always the same as the grammatical subject.
Use only one は per sentence; marking two nouns with は sounds odd unless you mean to contrast.
Once the topic is clear, Japanese often drops it entirely — you don't need to repeat 私は every sentence.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're looking at a photo with a friend, or pointing at something on a table, and you need to identify it. In English, you connect things to reality with "is", "am", or "are". In Japanese, you use one small word at the very end of your sentence: です—the copula (the word that works like *is/am/are*).

## How it works

Japanese sentences build backward compared to English. The core action or state always anchors the end. When you want to declare what something is, です lands at the finish line.

```jp
これはお茶[ちゃ]です。
```
*This is tea.*

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]です。
```
*I am a student.*

You don't always need to include the "This is" or "I am" part. If you're both looking right at a dog, you don't need to specify what you're talking about. You just say the noun and wrap it up with です.

```jp
犬[いぬ]です。
```
*It is a dog.*

## Time and truth

In English, "is" changes to "was" or "is not" depending on when it happened or if it's true. Japanese does the same thing, changing the shape of です.

To talk about the past, です becomes でした.

```jp
昨日[きのう]は学[がっ]校[こう]でした。
```
*Yesterday was school.*

To say something *isn't* the case, です becomes ではありません. We will give this negative form its own dedicated spotlight later, but you should start recognizing it now as the standard way to say "is not".

```jp
肉[にく]ではありません。
```
*It is not meat.*

## Rules and exceptions

The copula です attaches directly to nouns. You don't need any extra linking words between the noun and です.

> **Watch out:** You cannot stick です onto verbs to make them polite. Verbs have their own polite rules. Saying `食べるです` to mean "I politely eat" is a classic beginner trap.

## Casual speech

です is polite. You use it with teachers, strangers, and coworkers. But if you're talking to a close friend, です drops its polite suit and becomes だ.

```jp
水[みず]だ。
```
*It is water.*

Just be careful with it. だ sounds a bit punchy and emphatic. Often, in casual speech, people drop it entirely and just say the noun. But when you need to make a firm statement, だ is the actual casual equivalent of です.

That is the foundation of Japanese right there. Once you know how to declare that something *is*, you have the basic structure down. Hold onto this—soon we'll swap the ending for words like でしょう to say "It's probably water, right?"
caution_notes: Do not attach です directly to verbs like 食べる; verbs have their own separate polite forms.
だ is the casual form of です, but it can sound very punchy, so friends often just drop it completely.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are at a friend's house. They hand you a glass of clear liquid and you take a big gulp, expecting water. It burns. It is definitely not water. How do you tell them that?

## How it works

You already know the copula です (the little word that works like *is, am, or are*). In English, you negate a sentence by tossing "not" next to the verb. In Japanese, the copula itself shape-shifts to carry the negative meaning.

To say "is not" politely, you take a noun and attach either じゃないです or ではありません to it.

```jp
これは水[みず]じゃないです。
お酒[さけ]です。
```
*This is not water.*
*It is alcohol.*

Both じゃないです and ではありません mean the **exact same thing**, but they carry slightly different vibes. じゃないです is the standard, everyday polite form. It sounds natural in almost any spoken conversation. ではありません is much more formal and crisp. You will see it constantly in writing, but in speech, it sounds like you are giving a presentation or speaking to a strict boss.

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]ではありません。
```
*I am not a student.*

There is also a middle-ground spoken form: じゃありません. It feels a bit softer and slightly more traditional, but it is just as useful to recognize in daily life.

```jp
彼[かれ]は先[せん]生[せい]じゃありません。
```
*He is not a teacher.*

## Rules and exceptions

This pattern is incredibly common, but it has a strict diet: right now, you can only attach it to nouns.

> Do not try to attach じゃないです to a verb. If you want to say you aren't going to eat, you cannot say `食べるじゃないです`. Verbs have their own completely separate rules for becoming negative!

## Casual speech

When you are speaking casually with friends, the polite padding falls away completely. You drop the です or ありません and are left with just じゃない (or ではない in formal writing).

```jp
これは肉[にく]じゃない。
```
*This is not meat.*

Notice how the sentence ends abruptly. In casual Japanese, じゃない does all the heavy lifting on its own.

## Contrast

Let's line this up right next to what you already know. The structure of the sentence stays exactly the same; only the ending flips.

```jp
あれは学[がっ]校[こう]です。
あれは学[がっ]校[こう]じゃないです。
```
*That is a school.*
*That is not a school.*

Hold onto じゃない. You will see it pop up again later, attached to questions like じゃないですか to seek agreement and mean "isn't it?".
caution_notes: You can only attach ではありません or じゃないです to nouns (and na-adjectives, which you will learn later).
Never attach this pattern directly to a verb like 食べる.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're sitting with a new acquaintance at a café. You want to tell them you drink coffee. You know the word for coffee (コーヒー) and the word for drink (飲[の]む). But just saying `飲む` sounds a bit blunt, like you're talking to a close buddy. How do you dress it up for polite company?

## Making verbs polite

In English, we change our vocabulary to sound more polite. In Japanese, politeness happens at the very end of the sentence, attached directly to the verb. `ます` is your standard polite verb ending. It makes you sound respectful, safe, and friendly.

To use it, we have to prepare the verb by finding its "stem." Think of the stem as the verb's connector piece.

For many verbs, like `食べる` (to eat) or `見る` (to see), you simply drop the final `る` and attach `ます`.

```jp
私[わたし]はパンを食[た]べます。
```
*I eat bread.*

For other verbs, like `飲む` (to drink), `行く` (to go), or `買う` (to buy), the final `u` sound slides up to an `i` sound before adding `ます`. So `` `飲む` `` becomes `` `飲みます` ``, `` `行く` `` becomes `` `行きます` ``, and `` `買う` `` becomes `` `買います` ``.

```jp
コーヒーを飲[の]みます。
```
*I drink coffee.*

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。
```
*The teacher goes to school.*

```jp
明日[あした]、水[みず]を買[か]います。
```
*Tomorrow, I will buy water.*

And then there's `来る` (to come), which just breaks the rules and becomes `来ます`.

## Time and truth: ました and ません

Because `ます` is fused to the verb, it actually takes over the job of showing the tense (past or present) and whether the sentence is positive or negative.

You can swap `ます` for its past tense, `ました`, to talk about things that already happened.

```jp
昨日[きのう]、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。
```
*Yesterday, I watched a movie.*

To make a verb negative, swap `ます` for `ません`.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]は来[らい]ません。
```
*My friend is not coming.*

And for the past negative (did not do), we stack them into `ませんでした`.

```jp
今日[きょう]は本[ほん]を読[よ]みませんでした。
```
*I did not read a book today.*

## Rules and exceptions

The `ます` ending is strictly for action words. You cannot attach it to nouns or adjectives to make them polite.

Present tense in Japanese also covers the future. `食べます` means both "I eat" (as a habit) and "I will eat" (as a future plan). You don't need any extra words for "will".

> **Modify the ending first:** Never attach `ます` directly to the dictionary form of a verb. Forms like `` `食べるます` `` or `` `飲むます` `` are incorrect. You always have to change that final sound first!

## Casual speech

When you're talking to close friends or family, you don't use `ます` at all. You just use the raw, dictionary form of the verb. So `飲みます` (polite) drops back to just `飲む` (casual).

Since this is your first real verb ending, you'll use `ます` as your default whenever you're speaking to someone you aren't close friends with. You'll get plenty of dedicated practice with the negative and past forms (`ません` and `ました`) in the upcoming lessons. For now, hold onto this concept of a verb stem — it becomes very important when we start connecting verbs together with the te-form (て形[けい]) later on.
caution_notes: Never attach ます directly to the dictionary form of a verb; forms like 食べるます are incorrect.
ます is strictly for action words and cannot be attached to nouns or adjectives.

肉[にく]を食[た]べません。
今日[きょう]は行[い]きません。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are sitting across the table from your Japanese teacher. The conversation practice is wrapping up, and they gesture toward a fresh pot of coffee, asking if you want some. It is nine o'clock at night. You want to go to sleep soon, so caffeine is out of the question. You already know how to say that you *will* drink it by using the polite verb ending ます. But how do you express the exact opposite?

Shaking your head and just saying "no" works in a pinch, but you want to use your actual words. You need a way to tell your teacher that coffee and your sleep schedule do not mix, and you need to do it politely, without sounding brusque or dismissive.

This is where you need a way to turn a polite, affirmative verb into a polite negative. You need the workhorse ending ません.

```jp
私[わたし]はコーヒーを飲[の]みません。
```
*I do not drink coffee.*

## How it works: The modular swap

Japanese verb endings are incredibly modular. You can think of them like snapping blocks together. You already know how to build a polite, affirmative sentence using the ます ending. To make that exact same verb negative—to say "I do not" or "I will not"—you do not need to learn a whole new word. You just unclick the ます block from the end of the verb and snap on ません instead.

The first part of the verb—the "stem"—stays exactly the same. If the verb for drinking is 飲[の]みます, the stem is 飲[の]み. You keep that stem securely in place, drop the ます, and attach ません.

If you are at a restaurant and someone offers you a plate of meat, but you are a vegetarian, you simply take the verb 食[た]べます (to eat). Isolate the stem 食[た]べ, and attach your new negative ending to politely say you do not eat meat.

You can apply this to any verb you know. If your friend asks if you are going to school today, but you are staying home, you take 行[い]きます (to go) and swap the ending.

```jp
今日[きょう]、学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きません。
```
*I will not go to school today.*

Notice how the sentence structure feels completely familiar. The particles, the nouns, the time words—everything stays in its usual place. The only thing that changes is the very last sound of the sentence.

## Habit vs. future: Covering all your bases

One of the most frequent questions that trips up learners in their first month is how to distinguish between things they *never* do and things they are simply *not doing right now*.

In English, we say "I do not drink alcohol" to mean a general habit, and "I will not drink alcohol" to talk about tonight's party. Japanese does not make this grammatical distinction. The ません ending covers both. It handles your general, lifelong habits just as easily as it handles your immediate future plans.

How do you know which one it is? Context does all the heavy lifting for you.

```jp
お酒[さけ]を飲[の]みません。
```
*I will not drink alcohol.*

If someone points at a glass of beer right in front of you and asks if you want it, saying this sentence means you are refusing it right now. If someone asks you about your lifestyle in general, that exact same sentence simply means you are not a drinker. If you want to make it absolutely clear that you are talking about a specific time, you just add a time word to the sentence.

## The ultimate survival phrases

There are two specific negative verbs that you are going to use constantly, and they are worth memorizing right now as full phrases. When you are learning Japanese, there will be countless times when you do not catch what someone said, or when you are asked a question you do not have the answer to.

The verb 分[わ]かる means to understand. When a native speaker uses a word you have never heard, or talks just a little too fast, you need to be able to politely tell them you are lost.

```jp
分[わ]かりません。
```
*I do not understand.*

This is your safety cord. Pull it whenever you need the other person to slow down or explain things differently.

The other crucial verb is 知[し]る, which means to know. If someone stops you on the street and asks where the train station is, but you are a tourist yourself, you use the negative form of this verb: 知[し]りません.

It is easy to mix these two up, but try to remember the feeling of them. Use 分[わ]かりません when someone explains a complex problem or gives you instructions and your brain cannot process it. Use 知[し]りません when you simply do not possess the factual information, like the location of a friend's house.

## Inviting others: The power of a negative question

This is where ません goes from being a simple grammatical tool to an absolute social necessity. What happens if you take this negative ending and add the question particle か to the very end of it?

You might logically assume that ませんか simply means "Do you not do...?" And technically, on a purely literal level, it does. But in actual spoken Japanese, asking someone "Won't you do X?" is the single most common and natural way to invite them to do something with you.

Imagine you have a free afternoon tomorrow and you want to invite a friend to walk around the park with you. You could just say "Let's go," but Japanese culture values giving the other person space.

```jp
明日[あした]、一[いっ]緒[しょ]に公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きませんか。
```
*Won't you go to the park together tomorrow?*

By framing your invitation in the negative, you are structurally giving the other person an easy out. You are not demanding that they come; you are gently floating the idea. It leaves room for them to politely decline if they are busy.

If you are at a cafe and want to ask your friend if they would like something to drink, you use the exact same pattern, asking お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みませんか. This pattern is warm, polite, and considerate. When you want to initiate plans, this should be your go-to phrase.

## Looking back: The polite past negative

Everything we have talked about so far deals with the present or the future. But what happens when the action is already over? What if you want to confess that you did not do your reading, or tell a friend that you did not sleep last night?

To talk about something that did not happen in the past, ません has to stretch out a little bit. You take the standard ません ending and you add でした to the very end of it. The complete form becomes ませんでした.

You can think of this as stacking two different ideas: the negative block and the past tense block. It creates a longer, rhythmic ending.

```jp
昨日[きのう]、本[ほん]を読[よ]みませんでした。
```
*I did not read the book yesterday.*

Or perhaps someone asks if you saw the stray cat that usually hangs out near your house, and you reply 猫[ねこ]を見[み]ませんでした. It feels a bit long in your mouth at first, but because it follows the exact same mechanical rules as the present tense, your muscle memory will lock onto it quickly. Isolate the stem, and attach ませんでした.

## Rules and exceptions

> ません is strictly for verbs. You cannot attach it to nouns or adjectives.

This one trips everyone up the first week, so do not worry if you make this mistake once or twice—that is completely normal. Because ません is so incredibly useful, there is a strong temptation to stick it onto the end of everything.

If you want to say that the weather is not cold, you might look at the adjective 寒[さむ]い (cold) and try to say `寒いません`. Resist that urge. That sounds entirely broken to a native ear. The ません ending only ever snaps onto the stems of verbs. Nouns and adjectives have their own completely different rules for turning negative.

## Contrast: The suspense of the Japanese sentence

Let's put the affirmative and the negative side by side. Notice how the entire architecture of the sentence remains perfectly untouched. The subject, the time, the object—they all march in the exact same order. Only the very last syllables change.

```jp
今日[きょう]、海[うみ]に行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to the sea today.*

```jp
今日[きょう]、海[うみ]に行[い]きません。
```
*I will not go to the sea today.*

Because Japanese leaves the verb until the absolute end of the sentence, the listener doesn't actually know what the outcome is until the final moment. Are you going to the sea? Are you not going? The suspense builds up until the last split second.

The entire reality of your statement hinges on whether your sentence lands on ます or ません. This is why paying close attention to the end of a Japanese sentence is so crucial. If you tune out halfway through, you might completely miss whether someone just accepted or rejected your invitation.

Polite speech is an incredible tool. It keeps a safe, respectful distance between you and teachers, strangers, or store clerks. But what happens when you are hanging out with a close friend in your room? You wouldn't use this stiff, formal ません ending with them. Instead of swapping out the end block, you would change the very shape of the verb itself into a shorter, punchier form called the plain negative, or the ない形[かたち] (nai-form). Hold onto that thought—it completely changes how casual Japanese feels, and you will meet it very soon.
caution_notes: The ません ending is strictly for verbs; never attach it to nouns or adjectives.
Using ませんか at the end of a sentence is the standard polite way to invite someone to do something, meaning 'Won't you...?' rather than just acting as a negative statement.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this: it is Monday morning, and you are catching up with your Japanese teacher or a coworker. They casually ask how your weekend was. You want to tell them about the movie you watched, the delicious food you ate, or the friend you visited. 

But there is a problem. Right now, your Japanese toolkit only allows you to discuss the present and the future. If you try to tell them about the movie, you can only say `映画を見ます`—which tells them you *plan* to watch a movie. It does not help you share what already happened. To actually recount your experiences, tell stories, and connect over past events, you need a way to hit the rewind button on your verbs. You need the polite past tense.

## Shifting the Timeline

You are already intimately familiar with the polite verb ending `ます`. It is your reliable anchor for stating facts, declaring habits, and announcing future plans. The beautiful thing about Japanese verb conjugation—the way words change shape to express different meanings—is that it is heavily modular. It is a lot like clicking Lego pieces together. You do not have to memorize completely new, unpredictable words for the past tense the way you do in English (think of "eat" becoming "ate", or "buy" becoming "bought"). Instead, Japanese uses a predictable, mechanical swap.

To talk about the past, you take your standard polite verb, drop the `ます` completely, and attach `ました` in its place. That is it. The core of your verb—the stem, or the part of the word that carries the actual meaning of the action—stays completely untouched. We are just changing the grammatical bumper on the end to signal that the action is finished. Think about how powerful this is: if you can say "I will eat", you are only one syllable away from saying "I ate".

Let's look at the verb for "to read" as an example.

```jp
読[よ]む → 読[よ]みます → 読[よ]みました
```
*To read → read / will read → read (past).*

```jp
昨日[きのう]、本[ほん]を読[よ]みました。
```
*Yesterday, I read a book.*

Notice how clean that transition is. If you know the polite form of a verb, you automatically know its past tense form. There are no wild exceptions to this rule. Whether the verb is an everyday action like `食べる` (to eat) or a movement like `来る` (to come), the process is perfectly identical.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]は今日[きょう]、学[がっ]校[こう]に来[らい]ました。
```
*The teacher came to school today.*

## The Negative Past: What Didn't Happen

So, `ました` handles the things you actually did. But what about the things you skipped? The coffee you avoided, the book you did not finish, or the friend you did not meet? You need a way to express the negative past.

You already know that to say you *won't* or *don't* do something politely, you use the ending `ません`. To shift this negative reality backward in time, we do not replace `ません` entirely. Instead, we build right on top of it. You take `ません` and simply attach the word `でした` to the very end.

This creates the compound ending `ませんでした`. It functions as a single, unbreakable block that means "did not do".

```jp
飲[の]む → 飲[の]みません → 飲[の]みませんでした
```
*To drink → do not drink → did not drink.*

Let's apply it to a morning routine where you opted for water instead of your usual caffeine.

```jp
今日[きょう]、コーヒーを飲[の]みませんでした。
```
*I did not drink coffee today.*

This ending can feel a little intimidating at first. It is five full syllables long, which is quite a mouthful to stick onto the end of a verb. But its length is actually a secret weapon. Because it takes a moment to say, it gives your brain a valuable fraction of a second to plan your next thought while you are speaking. When you practice, do not just read it silently. Say it out loud until the rhythm feels completely natural. You will notice that in fast, fluent speech, native speakers often swallow the "shi" sound slightly, making it sound closer to a quick "ma-sen-desh-ta".

## Asking About the Past

Turning these past tense statements into questions is incredibly straightforward. Japanese does not require you to shuffle your word order around, and you do not need to add helper words like "did" to the beginning of the sentence. You just take your finished `ました` sentence, attach the question particle `か` to the very end, and let your voice rise slightly on the final syllable.

```jp
昨日[きのう]、友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]びましたか。
```
*Did you play with a friend yesterday?*

Answering these questions is just as smooth. Japanese thrives on efficiency and loves to drop any context that both speakers already understand. You do not need to repeat "yesterday" or "with a friend". You can just reply with a simple confirmation and the conjugated verb.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に遊[あそ]びました。
```
*We played together.*

## Playing with Time: Now and Today

Obviously, past tense verbs pair brilliantly with words that explicitly point backward, like `昨日` (yesterday). But Japanese gives you a lot of flexibility when it comes to framing time. You can absolutely use `ました` with a word like `今日` (today), provided the action is already over and done with. If it is five o'clock in the evening, your lunch is securely in the past.

Even more interestingly, you can use `ました` with the word `今` (now). In English, "now" feels strictly tied to the ongoing present moment. But in Japanese, combining `今` with a past tense verb creates the distinct feeling of an action having *just* been completed a second ago.

```jp
今[いま]、起[お]きました。
```
*I woke up just now.*

## Rules and Exceptions

The mechanics of `ました` are incredibly reliable, but there is one major grammatical trap you need to watch out for. This ending is strictly, exclusively, one-hundred-percent for action verbs.

> Because English uses the word "was" to handle the past tense for both nouns and adjectives ("The test was difficult," "He was a student"), it is very tempting to try and use `ました` the exact same way. You might logically think you can stick it onto `寒い` (cold) or `楽しい` (fun) to mean "It was cold" or "It was fun." Do not fall into this trap! Never say `寒いました` or `楽しいました`. This is one of the most common mistakes beginners make because their brains are translating English grammar directly into Japanese. But Japanese organizes the world differently. Adjectives and nouns belong to entirely separate grammatical families with their own unique rules for time travel. Keep `ました` securely locked to your action verbs.

## Casual Speech

It is important to remember that `ました` and `ませんでした`, just like their present-tense cousins, are inherently polite forms. They carry a baseline level of respect and social distance. You will use them constantly at work, in stores, with acquaintances, and with your teachers.

However, if you are hanging out at home with your partner or joking around with your closest friends, `ました` will suddenly feel stiff and unnatural. Using it in a very relaxed, intimate setting is almost like calling your best friend "Sir" or "Madam"—it creates an invisible wall of formality where there shouldn't be one. In those casual settings, the polite bumpers are dropped entirely, and the past tense takes on a completely different, shorter shape. You do not need to worry about that shape today, but it is good to be aware that `ました` is your "public facing" polite past tense.

## Contrast

To truly appreciate the power of what you have learned, look at the difference a single suffix makes. Let's line up the polite present and the polite past side by side.

```jp
今日[きょう]、肉[にく]を食[た]べます。
```
*Today, I will eat meat.*

```jp
昨日[きのう]、肉[にく]を食[た]べました。
```
*Yesterday, I ate meat.*

By simply swapping `ます` for `ました`, you completely rewrite the reality of the sentence. The first sentence is an intention; the meal has not happened yet. The second sentence is history; the plates are already cleared. When you are listening to spoken Japanese, train your ear to wait for that final syllable. That tiny structural shift is the only difference between an upcoming plan and a finished memory. Master `ます` for the things you will do, and `ました` for the things you have already done, and you instantly unlock the ability to share your life stories. Hold tightly onto this concept of shifting time—it is exactly the foundation you will need when we meet the casual plain past (the `た形`) a bit later on.
caution_notes: Never attach ました to Japanese adjectives or nouns, as they have their own completely separate rules for forming the past tense.
Since ました and ませんでした are inherently polite forms, using them with your closest friends or family can sound stiff and overly formal.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're walking around the park with an acquaintance. You're both tired and hungry, and you want to suggest getting some food. How do you step up and propose a plan?

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]にご飯[はん]を食[た]べましょう。
```
*Let's eat a meal together.*

## How it works

To make this "let's" form, you add ましょう to the **stem** of a verb. 

The stem is simply the core of the verb—the part you'd put before polite endings like ます. If you are building it directly from the dictionary form:

- For ru-verbs (like 食[た]べる or 見[み]る), drop the final る and add ましょう.
- For u-verbs (like 飲[の]む or 行[い]く), change that final 'u' sound to an 'i' sound (飲[の]む becomes 飲[の]み), then add ましょう.

```jp
学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きましょう。
コーヒーを飲[の]みましょう。
```
*Let's go to school.*
*Let's drink coffee.*

## Softening the suggestion (ましょうか)

If you add the question particle か to the end, you get ましょうか. This simple tweak does two very useful things.

First, it turns a confident "Let's" into a softer "Shall we?":

```jp
帰[かえ]りましょうか。
```
*Shall we go home?*

Second, it lets you offer your own help to someone else. If you see someone looking warm in a stuffy room, you can offer to fix it:

```jp
窓[まど]を開[あ]けましょうか。
```
*Shall I open the window?*

## Rules and exceptions

Because this pattern is all about proposing actions, you can only use it with things you actually have the power to do. 

> You can suggest "Let's wait here" (ここで待[ま]ちましょう), but you cannot say something like `分かりましょう` (Let's understand). If an action is out of your direct control, ましょう doesn't work.

```jp
ここで待[ま]ちましょう。
```
*Let's wait here.*

## Casual speech

ましょう is built for polite company—acquaintances, coworkers, or people you don't know perfectly well. When you are hanging out with close friends, Japanese drops this ending completely.

Instead, verbs morph into a shorter casual form (a volitional form) that usually ends in an "ou" sound. For example, 食[た]べましょう shrinks to `食べよう`, and 行[い]きましょう becomes `行こう`. You don't need to master those casual shapes today, but keep your ears open for them when friends talk to each other.

## Looking ahead

There is one slight catch to using ましょう. When you say "Let's watch a movie tomorrow," you are taking the lead. You are assuming the other person is basically on board.

```jp
明日[あした]、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ましょう。
```
*Let's watch a movie tomorrow.*

If you aren't sure if they want to, and you want to politely ask "Would you like to watch a movie?", you need a slightly different approach. That's where ませんか comes in. It lives in the exact same space, but offers the listener an easy way to say no. You'll meet it very soon, but for now, enjoy the confidence of ましょう. You're steering the ship.
caution_notes: You can only use ましょう with verbs that describe actions you can control; you cannot use it with verbs like 分かる (to understand).
ましょう is inherently polite, so it is used with colleagues or acquaintances rather than your closest friends.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing outside the theater with someone you like, the evening light going soft, and there's a movie you both keep mentioning. You don't want to *command* them to go — that feels heavy. You want to float the idea gently, leave the door open for them to say yes. Japanese has a beautiful move for exactly this: you phrase the invitation as a *negative* question.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか。
```

*Won't you watch a movie with me?*

Literally that's "won't you watch?" — and that softness is the whole point. By asking the negative, you're quietly signaling that a "no" is perfectly okay, which paradoxically makes people much more likely to say yes.

## How it works

The recipe is simple: take a verb, get its polite stem, and attach ませんか. You already know the polite negative ません (the "doesn't / won't" form). All you're doing is sticking a か on the end to turn that negative statement into a question.

Start from the polite form ます, swap it for ません, then add か:

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか。
```

*I watch a movie. / Won't you watch a movie?*

The pattern works with any verb the same way. Here's an invitation to have some tea:

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]にお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みませんか。
```

*Won't you have some tea with me?*

Notice how naturally 一[いっ]緒[しょ]に (together) rides along with this pattern. Invitations are almost always about doing something *with* someone, so 一[いっ]緒[しょ]に shows up constantly — think of them as travel companions.

And because it's a question, in speech your voice rises at the end, and in writing you'll often see a question mark even though か already does that job:

```jp
今日[きょう]、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか？
```

*Won't you watch a movie today?*

## Rules and exceptions

This is polite, invitation-flavored language. The ます part means you're already being polite, so ませんか is safe with people you don't know well, and warm rather than stiff with people you do.

Watch out for one trap: ませんか as an *invitation* is not the same as an ordinary negative question about facts. Context and intonation carry the difference, but as a learner, assume the "won't you...?" invitation reading whenever you're proposing an activity.

> ません on its own is just "doesn't / won't" — a flat negative statement. It's only the added か, plus an activity you'd plausibly do together, that turns it into an invitation. 映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ません means "I don't watch movies"; 映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか means "won't you watch a movie (with me)?"

Also, don't reach for the plain negative here. 見[み]ない is the casual "don't watch," but you can't just tack か onto it and get this same polite invitation flavor — ませんか is a set, polite package. Keep it whole.

## Casual speech

Among close friends, people often drop the polite machinery entirely and invite with a plain negative plus a rising tone:

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ない？
```

*Wanna watch a movie?*

That final 見[み]ない？ with the voice lifting up does the same social work as 見[み]ませんか — it's just stripped down and intimate. Same idea for tea: 一[いっ]緒[しょ]にお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]まない？ is the buddy-level version of 飲[の]みませんか. Use the ませんか form until you know the relationship is casual enough; overshooting into casual too early reads as presumptuous, while polite is never wrong.

## Contrast with ましょう

You already met ましょう — "let's / shall we." Both ませんか and ましょう invite, so what's the difference? It's all about how much of a "no" you're leaving room for.

ましょう assumes you're both basically on board and just seals the plan. ませんか opens the door and lets the other person decide — it's the more considerate first move.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ましょう。
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ませんか。
```

*Let's watch a movie (together). / Won't you watch a movie with me?*

A natural conversation often runs *through* both: you offer with ませんか, they say yes, and then you lock it in with ましょう. So they're not rivals — they're two beats of the same dance. Reach for ませんか when you're testing the waters, ましょう when the water's already warm.

Recap: verb stem + ませんか is your gentle, polite "won't you...?" invitation, softer than ましょう because it hands the choice to the other person. Hold onto that softening instinct — it comes back when we meet てください, where the tone you pick changes a request from an order into a favor.
caution_notes: ませんか is a polite, set invitation form — don't tack か onto the plain negative (見ない) and expect the same polite flavor.
ません alone is just a flat negative ('doesn't/won't'); it only becomes an invitation with か plus an activity you'd do together.
Use ませんか until you know the relationship is casual enough — polite is never wrong, but casual too early sounds presumptuous.

items.explanation_markdown:
Imagine it is early morning. You have just woken up, you stumble into the kitchen, and you pour yourself some coffee. If you want to describe this routine, you already know the word for coffee (コーヒー) and the verb for drinking (飲[の]む). 

But in Japanese, you cannot just shove a noun and a verb together and hope your listener figures it out. You need a way to tell them, "Hey, this coffee? It is the thing taking the hit. It is the target of my action."

In English, we rely entirely on the order of the words to know who is doing what. "I drink coffee" makes perfect sense, but "Coffee drink I" sounds like nonsense. Japanese, however, handles this completely differently. Instead of relying on a strict order, Japanese uses tiny grammatical tags attached to the ends of words to announce their job in the sentence.

Enter the particle を.

## How the object marker works

Think of を as a target reticle. It is a particle—a little word that attaches directly to the end of a noun—and its entire job is to point at an action and say, "The action happens to THIS."

Whenever you eat something, drink something, watch something, or buy something, the thing receiving that action gets the を particle.

```jp
コーヒーを飲[の]む。
パンを食[た]べる。
本[ほん]を読[よ]む。
```
*I drink coffee.*
*I eat bread.*
*I read a book.*

Typing and pronunciation note: When you are typing on a keyboard, you will type this character as "wo". However, in modern spoken Japanese, the "w" sound is almost entirely dropped. You will hear native speakers pronounce it exactly like the vowel "o" (お). It is a special character that exists almost exclusively to serve as this grammar particle.

## Building bigger sentences

Because particles like を act as permanent nametags for your words, it gives Japanese incredible flexibility. Let's bring back the topic marker は (the particle that means "as for X...") and see how they play together.

```jp
私[わたし]はお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]む。
彼[かの]女[じょ]は映[えい]画[が]を見[み]る。
```
*I drink tea.*
*She watches a movie.*

Notice the natural rhythm of a standard Japanese sentence: Topic は Object を Verb. The topic sets the stage at the beginning, the object receives the action in the middle, and the verb rigidly anchors the very end of the sentence.

But here is where the particle system shines. Because the particles are attached to the nouns, you can actually shuffle the order of the information before the verb, and the sentence still means the exact same thing.

```jp
私[わたし]は肉[にく]を食[た]べる。
肉[にく]を私[わたし]は食[た]べる。
```
*I eat meat.*
*As for the meat, I eat it.*

Both sentences mean you are eating meat. The second one just places a bit more emphasis on the meat by putting it first. Because を is glued to 肉[にく], and は is glued to 私[わたし], your listener never gets confused about who is eating and what is being eaten.

## Asking what someone is doing

You will use を constantly when asking people about their plans or their habits. If you want to ask "what" someone is doing, you combine the question word 何[なに] (what) with the を particle.

```jp
何[なに]を買[か]う？
明日[あした]、パンを買[か]う。
```
*What will you buy?*
*Tomorrow, I will buy bread.*

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]、何[なに]を見[み]る？
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]る。
```
*What do you watch every day?*
*I watch movies.*

> Notice how we didn't use the topic marker は for "you" or "I" in these examples? If you are looking right at your friend and asking a question, they already know you are talking to them. Japanese loves efficiency—if the topic is obvious from the context, you just drop it entirely and jump straight to the object and the verb.

## Rules and exceptions

There is one massive, unbreakable rule for を: it only ever works with action verbs.

You use it for eating, reading, buying, seeing, and listening. You absolutely **never** use it with the copula です (the word that works like *is/am/are*). 

If you want to say "It is water," you say `水です`. If you try to say `水をです`, you are basically saying "I am doing an action to the water... is." It is grammatical gibberish. Save を strictly for when a noun is actively having something done to it.

## Casual speech

Here is a messy truth about conversational Japanese that textbooks often hide until much later: when you are chatting casually with your friends, the を particle frequently vanishes into thin air.

When the context is totally clear, native speakers speak quickly and drop the object marker to save a syllable.

```jp
お酒[さけ]飲[の]む？
これ食[た]べる。
```
*Want to drink alcohol?*
*I'll eat this.*

Technically, these are `お酒を飲む？` and `これを食べる。`. While you are still building your muscle memory and getting used to how Japanese sentences are structured, you should practice using を every time. But do not be surprised when you hear your Japanese friends skipping it in casual situations.

## Contrast: は vs を

Because Japanese lets you omit so much information, it is completely normal for beginners to get confused about when to use the topic marker は and when to use the object marker を. 

Let's look at a sentence with both, and then see what happens if we mix them up.

```jp
猫[ねこ]は魚[さかな]を食[た]べる。
```
*The cat eats fish.*

Here, the cat (猫[ねこ]) is the topic. We are talking about the cat. The fish (魚[さかな]) is the target of the eating. The universe is in harmony.

But what if you panic and swap the particles?

```jp
魚[さかな]は猫[ねこ]を食[た]べる。
```
*The fish eats the cat.*

Now the fish is the topic (the one doing the action), and the cat is the one taking the hit! 

This is why particles are so vital. は sets the stage and introduces the main actor. を paints the target on the thing receiving the action. 

を is your absolute best friend for describing what you do to the world around you. You drink water, you read books, you meet friends. But what happens when something does an action *to* you? Or what if you want to emphasize exactly *who* is doing the action, rather than just treating them as a general topic? Hold onto that thought—it becomes incredibly important when we introduce the subject marker が a little later on.
caution_notes: を is only ever used with action verbs, never with the copula です.
In casual conversation, native speakers frequently drop the を particle entirely if the context is obvious.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're sitting in a quiet room and something moves in the corner. You want to say it out loud — "a cat!" — but not as the topic of a conversation, just pointing at the plain fact that a cat is *there*. This is the moment が was built for.

が is the subject marker: the little word that tags **who or what is actually doing the verb or being the thing**. Where は steps back and says "as for this, here's my comment," が leans in and points: *this one, right here, is the one.*

```jp
猫[ねこ]がいる。
```

*There's a cat.*

Notice there's no "as for" flavor here. You're not commenting on the cat as an already-known topic — you're announcing it. が does that announcing work.

## How it works

The structure is as simple as it looks: **Noun + が + Predicate**. The noun before が is the subject — the thing that exists, acts, or is described by whatever comes after.

The clearest place to feel が is with question words. When you ask *who* or *what* is doing something, you almost always reach for が, because you're asking the listener to fill in the unknown subject.

```jp
誰[だれ]がいる。
```

*Who's there?*

You can't make 誰[だれ] a topic — you can't comment on something you don't know yet. So は is off the table, and が steps in naturally. This is the single most reliable が instinct you can build: **question-word subjects take が.**

And the answer comes back with が too, because the answer is the newly-identified subject:

```jp
彼[かれ]がいる。
```

*He's there.*

が works the same way for existence and possession. When you're stating that something simply *exists* or that you *have* it, the thing that exists is marked with が.

```jp
お金[かね]がある。
```

*There's money. / I have money.*

Same shape every time: the thing being pointed at, then が, then the predicate. You don't conjugate が or change it — it's one fixed syllable doing one job.

## Rules and exceptions

The trap almost every learner falls into is reaching for が when they mean a general topic. If you're talking *about* yourself as the subject of an ongoing conversation, は is usually what you want. が is for the *new*, the *specific*, the *answer to a question* — the piece of information that wasn't already on the table.

> When a question word like 誰[だれ] or 何[なに] is the subject, use が, never は. "As for who?" is not a sentence.

There's a mirror rule that surprises people: the *answer* to a が question also takes が, but if you then shift to talking about that person generally, you switch back to は. The particle tracks what's new versus what's settled, not the grammar of the word itself.

> が marks the subject, but not every subject wears が. Once something becomes the known topic of the conversation, it often trades が for は.

## Casual speech

が itself doesn't contract — it's already a single clean syllable, so there's nothing to shorten. But in fast, casual speech, people often just *drop* it entirely when the meaning is obvious.

```jp
今[いま]、猫[ねこ]がいる。
猫[ねこ]いる。
```

*Right now, there's a cat. / A cat, there is.*

The first line is the full, neutral form. The second is what a friend might actually say pointing across the room — が gone, meaning intact. This dropping is casual only; in careful or polite speech, keep the が in.

## Contrast

Here's where が earns its keep against は, the topic marker you already know. Swap one for the other and the *feeling* of the sentence changes completely.

```jp
彼[かれ]がいる。
彼[かれ]は来[く]る。
```

*HE's the one who's here. / As for him, he'll come.*

The first line answers "who's here?" — が spotlights 彼[かれ] as the new, specific subject. The second uses は to set 彼[かれ] up as the topic and then comments about him. が points a finger; は sets a stage.

And against を, the direct object marker: を marks *what the action lands on*, while が marks *who does the action*. In a fuller sentence they'd sit on opposite sides of the verb — the doer in が, the done-to in を. For now, just hold the split: が is the actor, を is the target.

That's the whole core: が points at the subject, especially when it's new information or an answer to *who* or *what*. Hold onto this feeling — it comes back the moment we meet の and start linking nouns together.
caution_notes: When a question word like 誰 or 何 is the subject, use が — never は.
が marks new or specific subjects; once something becomes the known topic, it usually switches to は.
In casual speech が is often dropped entirely, but keep it in polite or careful sentences.

example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の本[ほん]です。

友[とも]達[だち]の車[くるま]です。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are sitting at a table with a classmate, and you notice a book left behind. You want to ask who it belongs to, or perhaps declare that it belongs to you. In English, you would use an apostrophe-s ('s) or the word "of". 

In Japanese, you handle this with a single, incredibly useful particle: の.

## How it works

The particle の is a linker. Its primary job is to connect two nouns together, turning them into one single noun block. The most common way you will use this is to show possession.

The rule is strict: the owner or describing noun always comes first, followed by の, and then the thing being owned or described.

```jp
これは誰[だれ]の本[ほん]ですか。
```
*Whose book is this?*

```jp
それは私[わたし]の本[ほん]です。
```
*That is my book.*

Just like in English, you can chain these connections together as much as you need to. You just keep inserting の between the nouns.

```jp
私[わたし]の友[とも]達[だち]の猫[ねこ]は魚[さかな]を食[た]べます。
```
*My friend's cat eats fish.*

## Dropping the obvious noun

Sometimes, repeating the noun feels clunky. If someone points to a coffee and asks whose it is, you do not need to reply "It is his coffee." You can just say "It is his."

Japanese does the exact same thing. You can drop the final noun completely, leaving の hanging at the end of the phrase, as long as the context makes it obvious what you are talking about.

```jp
このコーヒーは誰[だれ]のですか。
```
*Whose coffee is this?*

```jp
彼[かれ]のです。
```
*It is his.*

> When you drop the noun like this, の acts like "mine", "yours", "his", or "hers". Just remember that the item you are dropping must be clearly understood from the conversation.

## More than just ownership

Because Japanese rarely lets you smash two nouns directly together, you will use の for much more than just possession. It is the universal glue for any situation where one noun describes another.

If you want to say "Japanese teacher" or "school photographs", you cannot just say `日本語先生` or `学校写真`. You have to bridge them with の.

```jp
日本[にほん]語[ご]の先[せん]生[せい]は明日[あした]来[らい]ます。
```
*The Japanese teacher is coming tomorrow.*

```jp
学[がっ]校[こう]の写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]ます。
```
*I will look at photos of the school.*

## Don't mix up the order

The biggest trap for English speakers is reversing the order when translating phrases that use the word "of". In English, you say "the window of the room". The main thing (the window) comes first.

In Japanese, the main thing you are talking about always comes last. 

If you say `部屋の窓`, you are talking about the room's window. If you accidentally say `窓の部屋`, you are talking about a room made of windows. Always put the modifier first.

## The difference a particle makes

Since you already know は (the topic marker), let's look at how replacing it with の completely changes your sentence. 

```jp
私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]です。
```
*I am a friend.*

```jp
私[わたし]の友[とも]達[だち]です。
```
*(They are) my friend.*

The first sentence uses は to make "I" the topic of the whole sentence. The second sentence uses の to link "I" and "friend" into a single concept before the sentence even finishes.

Now you can talk about all the things that belong to you or your friends. Hold onto this ability to link words together—it will be crucial when we learn how to talk about going *to* a specific location, like a friend's house, using に next.
caution_notes: Always put the modifier first—Japanese doesn't let you reverse the order like the English 'of'.
You cannot drop the linking particle の when combining nouns, even for compound ideas like 'Japanese teacher'.
It is safe to drop the second noun (leaving just の) only when the context makes it obvious what item you are talking about.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's house and notice them putting on their coat. If you just ask 帰[かえ]りますか, it translates to "Will you go home?"—but it sounds a bit cold, like you're reading a survey question. You aren't just asking a random fact; you are seeing their coat and asking for an explanation based on that context. How do you ask "Oh, are you heading home?" with natural curiosity?

You use the explanatory んです.

```jp
帰[かえ]るんですか。
```
*Are you going home?*

### How it works

To build this, you take a verb in its plain, dictionary form (like 帰[かえ]る instead of 帰[かえ]ります) and add んです.

```jp
明日[あした]行[い]くんです。
```
*The thing is, I'm going tomorrow.*

To ask a question, you just add the question particle か to the end.

```jp
何[なに]を買[か]うんですか。
```
*What is it that you are buying?*

Why does this exist? Japanese has a tool called a *nominalizer*—a little word that turns an entire verb phrase into a noun-like thing you can talk about. Here, that word is の. When you add の to a verb, you turn "I go" into "The situation is that I go." 

In spoken Japanese, の often gets squished into ん, and we cap it off with です to make it polite. (In formal writing, you'll still see the unsquished version: のです).

### Casual speech

If you are talking to a friend and dropping です, this pattern changes slightly. The ん untangles back into a clear の, and you just raise your pitch at the end to make it a question.

```jp
今[いま]食[た]べるの？
```
*Are you eating now?*

```jp
どうして飲[の]まないの？
```
*Why aren't you drinking?*

> When answering casually, using a flat の at the end of a statement (行[い]くの。) can sound very soft or traditionally feminine. Men often use んだ instead, but when you're just starting out, simply replying with the plain verb (行[い]く。) is your safest bet.

### Reading the room

Because this pattern is all about explanations and shared context, it comes with a catch: you shouldn't use it for everything.

If you walk into a room and announce out of nowhere, 明日[あした]行[い]くんです (The thing is, I'm going tomorrow), people will wait for the rest of your story. It sounds like you are making an excuse or explaining a problem. Save it for when someone asks you why, or when you are reacting to something you both can see.

### Contrast: Invitations vs. Explanations

Let's look at how this fits with what you already know. You learned that adding ませんか to a verb stem makes a polite invitation. It looks similar to asking a negative んです question, but the meaning is totally different.

```jp
コーヒー、飲[の]みませんか。
```
*Won't you drink some coffee?*

```jp
コーヒー、飲[の]まないんですか。
```
*Are you not drinking coffee?*

The first invites them to drink. The second notes that they don't have a cup, and asks for the reason why.

Mastering んです is the key to sounding like you're actually participating in a conversation rather than just reading textbook sentences at people. Hold onto this feeling of modifying the ends of verbs—it becomes incredibly important when we look at ongoing actions with ている later on!
caution_notes: Using んです on every single sentence sounds like you are constantly making excuses; save it for when you need to explain something or react to shared context.
In casual speech, declarative statements ending in a flat の can sound traditionally feminine, so answering simply with the plain verb is often safer.

items.mnemonic_text: に pins an action to a point in time or a destination.

example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。
七[なな]時[じ]に起[お]きます。
友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]います。
椅[い]子[す]に座[すわ]ります。
日本[にほん]に住[す]んでいます。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are making weekend plans. You want to tell your friend you are heading to the park, and you want to ask what time they usually wake up. To say *where* you are going or *when* an event happens, you need a way to pinpoint that information. In Japanese, we use the particle に.

## How it works

Think of に as a dart. You throw it, and it lands on a specific, fixed target. That target can be a place on a map, a specific time on a clock, or even a person.

First, let's throw the dart at a map. When you use motion verbs like 行[い]く (to go) or 帰[かえ]る (to return home), に attaches to the place to mark your exact destination.

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。
```
*I go to school.*

```jp
彼[かれ]は家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ります。
```
*He returns home.*

Next, throw the dart at a calendar or a clock. に attaches to specific times to say exactly *when* an action happens.

```jp
何[なに]時[じ]に起[お]きますか。
```
*What time do you wake up?*

```jp
日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]に公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to the park on Sunday.*

Finally, you can throw the dart at a person. When an action is directed at someone—like meeting them or asking them a question—に marks that person as your target.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]います。
```
*I meet a friend.*

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]に聞[き]きます。
```
*I ask the teacher.*

## Rules and exceptions

Here is where に gets tricky, and it trips everyone up the first week—that's normal! You cannot just put に after *every* time word.

Remember how に is a dart hitting a fixed target? Some time words are relative. "Tomorrow" (明日[あした]) changes depending on when you say it. "Today" (今日[きょう]) is a floating concept, not a fixed number on a clock or calendar. Because they aren't fixed points, they reject the に dart.

> Relative time words like 今日[きょう] (today), 明日[あした] (tomorrow), and いつ (when) never take に.

So, you just leave them bare in the sentence:

```jp
明日[あした]、学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to school tomorrow.*

## Casual speech

In casual, everyday conversation, Japanese speakers often drop particles completely if the meaning is obvious. The destination に is one of the first to disappear when you are talking to friends.

```jp
明日[あした]、公[こう]園[えん]行[い]く？
```
*Are you going to the park tomorrow?*

## に vs を

You learned を (the direct object particle) for the thing you physically act upon. Compare these two sentences:

```jp
水[みず]を飲[の]みます。
```
*I drink water.*

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]います。
```
*I meet a friend.*

In the first sentence, water is the object you are directly consuming. In the second, your friend is the *target* you are directing your "meeting" action toward. You aren't "consuming" your friend! That is why interaction verbs like 会[あ]う (to meet) and 聞[き]く (to ask/listen) take the target particle に, not the direct object を.

Whether it's a place, a time, or a person, に is your trusty dart for hitting the target. Hold onto this concept of a destination—soon you will meet へ, a particle that lives in the same space but cares more about the journey than the exact landing spot.
caution_notes: Relative time words like 'today' or 'tomorrow' do not take the に particle because they are not fixed points in time.
Interaction verbs like 会う (to meet) and 聞く (to ask) take the target particle に, not the direct object particle を.

items.mnemonic_text: へ points the way you are heading.

example_sentences.furigana: 東[とう]京[きょう]へ行[い]きます。
家[いえ]へ帰[かえ]ります。
学[がっ]校[こう]へ来[らい]ました。

example_sentences.english: I want to go to the sea.
example_sentences.furigana: 海[うみ]へ行[い]きたいです。

items.explanation_markdown:
You pack your bag and step out the door. The weather is beautiful, and you're heading toward the park. How do you describe that trajectory—the physical direction you are moving in?

```jp
私[わたし]は公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。
```
*I am heading to the park.*

## How it works

To mark the direction you are traveling, attach the particle へ directly to your destination noun. It works almost exclusively with movement verbs like `行く` (to go), `来る` (to come), and `帰る` (to return).

> When reading, this character is written as へ (he), but when used as a particle, it is always pronounced "e" (like the "e" in "elephant"). You already saw this quirk when the character は became the topic particle "wa".

The structure is always the place you are heading toward, followed by へ, followed by the movement.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]が学[がっ]校[こう]へ来[らい]ます。
```
*The teacher comes to the school.*

```jp
明日[あした]、海[うみ]へ行[い]きます。
```
*Tomorrow, we will head to the sea.*

```jp
彼[かれ]は家[いえ]へ帰[かえ]ります。
```
*He is returning home.*

## Rules and exceptions

Because へ is an arrow pointing outward, it only makes sense when there is actual physical movement involved. You cannot use it to describe where an action takes place if you are staying still. For example, you cannot say `部屋へ本を読みます` to mean reading a book inside a room.

Additionally, while the particle に can attach to a time word to mark when something happens, へ is strictly spatial. You cannot attach it to a time word to say something like `何時へ行きますか` (toward what time are you going?).

## Contrast: The arrow vs. the thumbtack

If you're thinking, "Wait, didn't I already learn に for going to a place?", you are absolutely right. 

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。
```
*I go to the park.*

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。
```
*I head toward the park.*

In modern, everyday spoken Japanese, these two sentences are practically interchangeable. Most of the time, nobody will bat an eye if you use に instead of へ when talking about your destination.

The difference is nuance. に acts like a thumbtack on a map—it focuses strictly on the final endpoint. へ acts like an arrow—it highlights the direction of travel and the journey itself. Because it draws attention to the path, へ can sometimes sound a bit more sweeping or poetic. It is also common in formal announcements (like a train heading toward a specific station).

Remember: へ points the arrow, and に marks the spot. Hold onto this spatial logic, because you will soon meet で—a particle that builds the stage for where actions actually happen once you arrive.
caution_notes: The particle へ is always pronounced 'e' (like in elephant), not 'he'.
Use へ exclusively with movement verbs (like 行く, 来る, 帰る); it cannot be used for stationary actions.
Unlike に, you cannot attach the direction particle へ to a time word.

items.explanation_markdown:
You've got your weekend plans sorted. You know what you want to do and what you want to eat. But if a friend asks exactly where all this is happening, or how you plan to get there, you're going to need the particle で.

で attaches directly to the end of a noun. It operates like a tag that tells your listener about the background details of your action.

## Setting the stage

When you do an active verb—like reading, eating, or watching a movie—you need a stage for that action to happen on. You mark that location with で. Think of it as answering "where is this event taking place?"

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]、図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]む。
```
*On the weekend, I read books at the library.*

```jp
家[いえ]で映[えい]画[が]を見[み]る。
```
*I watch movies at home.*

```jp
これ、どこで買[か]う？
```
*Where do you buy this?*

## Marking the tool

The second job of で is marking the means or method of an action. It tells us what tool you used to get the job done. In English, this usually translates to "by" or "with".

```jp
バスで学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]く。
```
*I go to school by bus.*

```jp
箸[はし]で魚[さかな]を食[た]べる。
```
*I eat fish with chopsticks.*

## The "at" trap: で vs. に

This one trips everyone up the first week—that's completely normal. In English, we use "at" or "in" for almost everything location-related. Japanese splits the job between で and the particle に you learned earlier.

に acts like a dart hitting a dartboard. It marks a destination you are moving toward, but it doesn't describe a stage where a full activity takes place. If you are traveling toward a place, use に (or へ). If you are actively doing something once you get there, use で.

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]く。
```
*I go to the park.*

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]ぶ。
```
*I play at the park.*

> Be careful: if you try to say `公園に遊ぶ`, a Japanese speaker will be very confused. You can't "play toward" a park!

So で handles the "where" and the "by what means". But what if you want to say you watched a movie *with* a friend? Don't use で here. Tools take で, but companions take a different particle entirely. Hold onto that thought—it becomes important when we meet と later.
caution_notes: Use で for the location where an action takes place, not に.
Don't use で to say you are doing something with a person; it is strictly for tools and means.

items.mnemonic_text: と ties a full list of nouns or a companion together.

example_sentences.furigana: パンと卵[たまご]を買[か]います。
友[とも]達[だち]と行[い]きます。

example_sentences.english: There are a dog and a cat.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]がいます。
先[せん]生[せい]と話[はな]します。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're sitting at a cozy diner in Tokyo, and you want to order a nice breakfast. You know the words for coffee, bread, and eggs. You could just point and say the words one by one, hoping the waiter understands you want them all.

But that feels a bit choppy, like a robot reading a grocery list. You want to sound like a human, smoothly connecting your thoughts. In English, you'd just use the word "and." It's one of the first words we master as children, endlessly chaining our thoughts together.

In Japanese, the most common equivalent is the particle と. It is small, it is incredibly common, and it is going to immediately make your sentences sound far more natural. But there is a catch. The Japanese と has a very specific personality, and it handles a second job that might surprise you.

## Connecting the dots

Let's start with its most basic job. When you want to bundle two physical things together, you place と right between them. It acts exactly like a plus sign (+) in mathematics, sitting squarely between two nouns.

```jp
パンと卵[たまご]
```
*Bread and eggs.*

It doesn't change the words around it, and it doesn't require any special conjugation. You simply drop it in. This means you can string more than two things together if your list is getting long. You just keep inserting a new と after every single noun, like links in a chain.

```jp
肉[にく]と魚[さかな]と卵[たまご]を買[か]います。
```
*I will buy meat, fish, and eggs.*

Look closely at how that sentence flows. The particle と bundles all three of those food items together into one giant noun phrase. Then, the direct object particle を steps in. It marks that entire bundle as the single target of the verb "to buy". You don't need a separate を for the meat and the fish; the と linked them up so they could share it.

When you are pointing at a menu or trying to explain what you need, combining demonstrative words (like "this" and "that") with と is incredibly powerful.

```jp
これとそれを使[つか]います。
```
*I will use this one and that one.*

This instantly elevates your ability to communicate your choices. You aren't just pointing and grunting anymore; you are building a proper grammatical structure that tells the listener exactly what you intend to do with multiple items.

## "With" someone

Now we arrive at the feature that often surprises English speakers. In English, the concepts of "and" and "with" feel fundamentally different. We think of "and" as a way to list things, and "with" as a way to show accompaniment.

But Japanese looks at the underlying logic. If you say "my friend and I will go," you are describing a situation where two people are traveling together. That is functionally identical to saying "I will go with my friend."

Because of this shared logic, the particle と handles both jobs perfectly.

```jp
私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]と公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to the park with a friend.*

When you attach と directly to a person or an animal, and then follow it up with an action, it naturally translates to "together with." You do not need to hunt for a separate vocabulary word for "with". The particle itself carries all the weight.

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]、お父[ちち]さんとお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みます。
```
*Every day, I drink tea with my father.*

This pattern is incredibly versatile. Whether you are studying with a classmate, living with a sibling, or just walking with your dog, と is the particle you need. If you want to be completely unambiguous and emphasize the "togetherness" of the action, you can pair it with the vocabulary word 一[いっ]緒[しょ]に (together).

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。
```
*I will watch a movie together with my girlfriend.*

You will hear this specific combination constantly in daily Japanese conversation. It adds a nice sense of warmth and cooperation to the sentence.

## The boundaries of と

This is the part of the lesson where English speakers usually stumble, because our English brains try to trick us. Because we use the English word "and" for absolutely everything, we assume we can sprinkle と everywhere too. But Japanese grammar is much stricter about categorizing words.

> The golden rule of と is that it can only connect nouns. You can never use it to link verbs, adjectives, or entire sentences.

Let's say you are describing your weekend plans. You want to say, "I will eat and sleep." It is extremely tempting to take the verbs for eat and sleep and just stick と between them. But if you say `食べると寝る`, a native Japanese speaker will look at you with total confusion. In their mind, you just tried to use a physical plus sign to combine two actions. It feels structurally broken. This particle is strictly reserved for bridging things, people, places, or ideas. You will learn completely different grammar patterns for linking actions or describing a sequence of events later in your journey.

The second major boundary is that と is strictly exhaustive. When you use it, you are presenting a complete, closed list.

```jp
犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]
```
*A dog and a cat.*

When you say this phrase, you are stating that there is a dog and a cat, and *absolutely nothing else*. If you were at a pet store and there were also birds and fish present, using と here means you are actively excluding them from your statement. It paints a closed box with only the mentioned items inside. If the listener opens the box, they expect to find exactly a dog and a cat, no more, no less.

## と versus で (The two "withs")

Because English uses the single word "with" in two completely different ways, you have to run a quick mental check when translating your thoughts into Japanese. Think about the difference between the sentences "I ate with a friend" and "I ate with chopsticks."

In the first sentence, the friend is a companion sharing the experience. In the second sentence, the chopsticks are merely a tool you are wielding to accomplish the task. You already know the particle で, which marks the tool, means, or method you use.

```jp
お金[かね]で本[ほん]を買[か]います。
```
*I buy books with money.*

Here, money is the tool you are using to facilitate the purchase. If you accidentally used と in this situation and said `お金と本を買います`, you would completely change the meaning. You would be telling the shopkeeper, "I will buy money and books." They might wonder how exactly one goes about purchasing money.

When you want to mark a living companion who is joining you in the action, you must always use と.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]と本[ほん]を買[か]います。
```
*I will buy books with a friend.*

Before you speak, ask yourself: Are you using this object to accomplish a task? Use で. Is this person or animal keeping you company? Use と.

## と versus に (Targets vs Partners)

You have also learned the particle に, which acts as a target or a direction for your action. Sometimes, swapping に for と completely changes the social dynamic of what is happening in the sentence.

Let's imagine you are confused at a train station and you need to ask someone for directions.

```jp
駅[えき]員[いん]に聞[き]きます。
```
*I will ask the station staff.*

In this sentence, に acts like an arrow pointing your question directly at the station staff. They are the clear target of your action. But watch what happens if you accidentally swap that particle for と.

```jp
駅[えき]員[いん]と聞[き]きます。
```
*I will listen with the station staff.*

Suddenly, the entire scenario has shifted. You and the station staff are now partners, standing side-by-side, listening to someone else speak! The particle に directs the action *at* someone, while と pulls them alongside you to experience it together.

This exact same shift happens with verbs involving meeting people.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]に会[あ]います。
```
*I will meet the teacher.*

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]と会[あ]います。
```
*I will meet with the teacher.*

Both of these sentences are perfectly natural Japanese, and they are often used interchangeably in casual speech. However, using に feels a bit more one-sided—you are going to the teacher, perhaps because they called you into their office. Using と implies mutual coordination. It feels like you both checked your calendars, agreed on a time, and chose to meet up as equals.

## Casual speech notes

Unlike some of the heavier grammar patterns you will encounter later, the particle と itself doesn't contract or change shape in casual speech. It remains perfectly intact whether you are speaking formally to a boss or casually to a close friend. 

What *does* change is how often it gets dropped entirely. In very fast, casual Japanese, speakers will sometimes just list nouns with a slight pause between them instead of explicitly using と (saying "pan, tamago" instead of "pan to tamago"). But as a learner, you should always keep it in your toolkit to ensure you are understood clearly.

## Wrapping up

The particle と is the foundational glue you need to start building more complex, descriptive sentences, as long as you remember to only stick nouns together. Whenever you need to list your favorite foods, or talk about who is joining you for a weekend trip, this is the tool you will reach for.

Just remember that it always creates a closed, complete list. If you want to say things like "meat, fish, and things like that" without sounding like you're reciting a strict legal inventory, you'll need a slightly softer particle. Hold onto that thought—we will meet the open-ended particle や in a future lesson to solve exactly that problem.
caution_notes: と can only connect nouns, never verbs or sentences.
Lists made with と are exhaustive; they imply nothing else is included.
