You just walked into a massive, sprawling shopping mall. The store shelves are overflowing with hundreds of different sections, and you spend an entire afternoon just browsing. Later that evening, a friend asks you what you looked at.

If you try to list every single thing you saw, you are going to be talking for a long, long time. You don't want to recount the entire floor plan of the building. You just want to give them a sampler platter of your day: "I looked at books and magazines, things like that."

When you first start learning a language, you often feel a bit like a lawyer. You have to be overly precise because your grammatical toolbox is still small. If someone asks what you did or what you saw, you try to list every single thing to be completely accurate. Alternatively, you leave things out and feel a slight twinge of guilt, as if you are hiding the truth.

But native speakers do not talk like lawyers in their everyday lives. They speak in broad, relaxed strokes. They give a few key details, a couple of prominent examples, and then they let the listener's imagination fill in the rest of the gaps.

You already know how to use the particle `と` to say "and." But `と` has a massive catch: it creates a closed, airtight loop. If you say you looked at books `と` magazines, you are telling your friend that you looked at exactly those two things, and absolutely nothing else in the entire store. If you actually looked at photographs as well, using `と` makes your statement technically untrue.

When you want to give a few examples without claiming it is the whole exhaustive list, you need a different grammatical tool. Enter the particle `や`.

## How the open list works

The particle `や` sits right between two nouns, in the exact same physical spot where `と` would normally go. But instead of locking the list down and throwing away the key, `や` props the door wide open. It tells your listener, "Here are a couple of examples of what is going on, but please do not hold me to this being everything."

```jp
本[ほん]や雑[ざっ]誌[し]を読[よ]みます。
```
*I read books, magazines, and things like that.*

By using `や` instead of `と`, you leave a little ghost space at the end of your sentence. The listener inherently knows that there might also be newspapers, manga, or internet articles involved in your reading habits, even though you did not bother to explicitly name them.

Sometimes, you want to make that "ghost space" a little more obvious. You can do this by sticking the word `など` at the very end of your list, right after the final noun. The word `など` translates roughly to "etcetera," "and so on," or "and the like."

```jp
朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]にパンや果物[くだもの]などを食[た]べます。
```
*I eat bread, fruit, and the like for breakfast.*

Adding `など` does not dramatically change the core meaning of the sentence—the `や` already did the heavy lifting of making the list open-ended—but it rounds out the phrasing beautifully. It acts like a little verbal wave of the hand, confirming out loud that the list trails off into other unspoken items. You will hear native speakers use this combination constantly.

Grammatically, when you use `Noun A + や + Noun B`, Japanese treats that entire clustered chunk as one single, giant mega-noun. The grammatical machinery that comes afterward—like the object marker `を` or the subject marker `が`—does not care how many items are packed inside that basket. It just attaches to the very end of the cluster (or to `など`, if you used it) and treats the whole thing exactly the same way it would treat a single, solitary word.

## The rules of the sampler platter

Japanese grammar is notoriously strict about keeping different kinds of words in their own separate lanes. English is quite lazy by comparison. In English, the word "and" is a universal Swiss Army knife. We use it to connect nouns ("cats and dogs"), adjectives ("big and red"), and verbs ("I ate and slept").

Japanese absolutely does not work this way. The most important rule you must remember for `や` is that it **only connects nouns**.

You cannot use it to connect adjectives, and you absolutely cannot use it to connect verbs. If you want to say that you wake up and eat, you have to use an entirely different grammatical machine. Using `起きるや食べる` is a fast track to sounding completely broken. A native speaker will hear the `や` and immediately expect another noun; when a verb comes out instead, their brain will skip a beat. Keep this particle strictly confined to people, places, and things.

> You might be tempted to string together four, five, or six nouns with `や`, just like you might freely do in English ("I bought apples and bananas and oranges and grapes"). Resist this urge. In Japanese, chaining more than two or three items with `や` sounds extremely clunky, robotic, and overwhelming. Give two strong examples and let the particle do the rest of the unspoken work.

Let's look at another scenario, this time using locations instead of objects. You are planning your weekend out in the city and chatting with a coworker about your plans.

```jp
明日[あした]、海[うみ]や公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。
```
*Tomorrow, I will go to the sea, a park, and so on.*

This paints a picture of a relaxed, flexible, and open itinerary. If you end up going to a movie theater or a coffee shop as well, you haven't broken any promises or lied about your weekend, because the `や` kept your schedule completely open to additions.

## The closed box vs. the open basket

Because you now have two different ways to say "and" with nouns, let's put them right next to each other so you can truly feel the difference. This is what language teachers call a minimal pair: two sentences that are completely identical except for the one single piece of grammar we are swapping out.

First, let's look at the particle you already know, the exhaustive (closed list) `と`.

```jp
今日[きょう]、肉[にく]と魚[さかな]を買[か]います。
```
*Today, I will buy meat and fish.*

Think of `と` as a closed box. Imagine you are running an errand for a very strict chef. If you give them this sentence, you are stating as an absolute fact that your entire grocery purchase will consist of meat and fish, and absolutely zero other items. There is no room for interpretation. If you also buy vegetables, you have violated the boundaries of the `と` box.

Now, swap in our new pattern, `や`.

```jp
今日[きょう]、肉[にく]や魚[さかな]などを買[か]います。
```
*Today, I will buy meat, fish, and so on.*

This is the open basket. If you are just describing your general grocery shopping plans to a friend, this is the one you want to use. It means that meat and fish are the headliners of your shopping trip, but you are probably also going to pick up some water, maybe some vegetables, or whatever else catches your eye. You are simply painting a general picture of your errands.

If you are ever trying to decide which one to use in a live conversation, take a split second to ask yourself: "Am I giving an exact, restricted inventory, or am I just giving a few examples?" If it is a strict inventory, use `と`. If it is just a sampler platter, reach for `や`.

## Casual speech and structural glue

In casual Japanese, especially when you are speaking quickly with close friends, you probably already know that speakers love to drop grammatical particles. Target markers like `に`, object markers like `を`, and subject markers like `が` frequently vanish into thin air when the context makes it obvious what is happening.

However, `や` is structural glue. It holds the core meaning of the nouns together, so it does not get dropped.

Imagine you are hanging out with a friend, and they ask what you usually drink on a hot day.

```jp
水[みず]やお茶[ちゃ]飲[の]む。
```
*I drink water, tea, and so on. (Casual)*

Notice how the object marker `を` is completely gone, which is incredibly common in casual speech, but the `や` remains untouched. It is essential for letting your friend know that water and tea are just a few options among many.

## Connecting people

Finally, keep in mind that this open basket is not just for objects and places. `や` works beautifully with people, too. Imagine you are at a large school event and you are describing the massive crowd gathering in the courtyard.

```jp
学[がっ]校[こう]で先[せん]生[せい]や学[がく]生[せい]に会[あ]います。
```
*I meet teachers, students, and others at school.*

You might also meet parents, station staff, or police officers on your commute, but teachers and students are the primary groups you are choosing to highlight. The target particle `に` clips right onto the end of the `先生や学生` block without skipping a beat.

Hold onto this concept of making open-ended lists. Right now, you are building these lists with `や`. Soon, you will meet the particle `も` (also / too), which you can use to explicitly stack even more additions onto these kinds of open-ended scenarios. Until then, enjoy the freedom of not having to list every single noun in your vocabulary!
caution_notes: The particle や can only connect nouns; never use it to connect adjectives or verbs.
Chaining more than two or three nouns with や sounds unnatural—stick to a few strong examples and let the particle imply the rest.

You are out grabbing drinks with a friend at a local cafe. They step up to the counter, look at the menu, and order a coffee. You are next in line, and honestly, a coffee sounds perfect to you right now too. 

In English, you have a few easy ways to express this shared feeling. You might say, "I'll have a coffee too," or simply agree with a quick, "Me too." 

In Japanese, expressing this is incredibly straightforward. You use the particle も to add that precise "also" or "too" nuance to your sentence. It is one of the most common and useful tools you will learn, because it instantly makes your speech sound connected to the people around you.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]はコーヒーを飲[の]みます。
私[わたし]もコーヒーを飲[の]みます。
```
*My friend will drink coffee.*
*I will also drink coffee.*

## How it works

Whenever you want to show that a new person, place, or thing shares a trait or performs the exact same action as something that was already mentioned, you bring in も. You attach it right after the noun you want to elevate.

But here is the most important mechanical rule to remember: this particle completely devours the basic marker particles. You already know は (the topic marker), が (the subject marker), and を (the object marker). When も steps onto the stage, those basic markers vanish.

If you want to say "I am a student too," you do not stack the particles together. You never say `私はも` or `私もは`. The new particle just steps in and takes over the job completely.

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]です。
彼[かれ]も学[がく]生[せい]です。
```
*I am a student.*
*He is also a student.*

Why does Japanese do this? Think of basic particles like は and が as structural scaffolding. They hold the sentence up. But も is a spotlight. When you shine that spotlight on a noun, everyone already knows it is the main subject based on context, so the language prioritizes the "also" feeling over the rigid grammatical scaffolding.

This devouring rule works exactly the same way when you are dealing with the objects of a sentence. Imagine you are at a store. You decide to buy a book, but then you see a movie on the shelf next to it that you also want. You are performing the exact same action on a second object.

Instead of using the object marker を for the movie, you simply swap it out.

```jp
本[ほん]を買[か]います。
映[えい]画[が]も買[か]います。
```
*I will buy a book.*
*I will buy a movie too.*

It is wonderfully efficient. The listener already knows what action is happening, and by simply dropping in も, you seamlessly add another item to the list of things being bought.

## Rules and exceptions

> **Watch out:** English gives you a lot of freedom to float the word "also" around a sentence. You can say "I also drink water," or "I drink water also." Japanese is strictly rigid in its structure. The particle も must physically attach directly to the noun it is talking about.

There is another fantastic feature of this particle that trips up learners at first, but makes perfect sense once you see it in action. When you use it in a negative sentence, the meaning naturally shifts to "neither" or "not either."

Because Japanese verbs carry the negative meaning at the very end of the sentence, the particle itself does not need to change. You just swap out the topic or object marker exactly as you did before, and the negative verb takes care of the rest.

```jp
今日[きょう]は肉[にく]を食[た]べません。
魚[さかな]も食[た]べません。
```
*I will not eat meat today.*
*I will not eat fish either.*

This is often a huge relief for English speakers. In English, we have to learn entirely new vocabulary words to handle negatives—"also" turns into "neither", and "too" turns into "either". Japanese does not make you memorize a new set of negative grouping words. It trusts you to use the exact same building blocks and just flip the verb to negative at the end.

## Contrast: も vs. と

Since you are learning how to group things together, it is very common to wonder how this new particle compares to the particle と, which you already know means "and."

While they seem somewhat similar when translated, they serve very different purposes in a Japanese conversation. The particle と groups multiple things together into one tidy, closed package. It implies you are looking at the whole group at once.

On the other hand, も adds new information to an established pattern. It is a follow-up. You establish a fact first, and then you use it to say, "Hey, this other thing fits that fact as well."

Let's look at the difference when talking about animals at the park.

```jp
犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]を見[み]ます。
```
*I see a dog and a cat.*

In that sentence, you are observing both animals in one single thought. Now look at how the feeling changes when we split it up.

```jp
犬[いぬ]を見[み]ます。
猫[ねこ]も見[み]ます。
```
*I see a dog.*
*I see a cat too.*

Here, you noticed the dog first. That was your established action. Then, you noticed the cat, and you wanted to emphasize that the cat shares the exact same action as the dog. It feels much more conversational and layered.

When you are first starting to speak Japanese, you might feel like you are just firing off isolated, robotic sentences. Learning this particle is your first big step toward sounding like a natural participant in a conversation. It allows you to piggyback on what other people are saying and build a bridge between speakers.

For now, spend your time practicing swapping out those basic markers when you want to say "too." Keep this versatile little word in your back pocket. Later on in your studies, you will see how it can stack with other directional particles like から (from) to mean things like "even from," but you already have the core pattern down perfectly.
caution_notes: Remember that も completely replaces the basic marker particles は, が, and を, rather than stacking with them.
Unlike English where 'also' can float around the sentence, the particle も must physically attach directly to the noun it modifies.

You're at a welcome party for new students and someone asks where you traveled from, or a friend wants to know when your new schedule starts. How do you mark the starting point of your journey or your time?

## How it works

To express "from" a place or a time, Japanese uses the particle から (a little word that attaches to nouns to show their grammatical role). It works like a thumbtack on a map or a calendar, pinning down the exact starting point of whatever action you are talking about.

You just attach it directly to the end of the noun. Remember that Japanese particles always come *after* the word they modify. So "from here" becomes "here from" (ここから).

```jp
どこから来[らい]ましたか。
```
*Where did you come from?*

```jp
家[いえ]から歩[ある]きます。
```
*I will walk from home.*

It works exactly the same way for time. If an action starts at a specific moment, just attach から to that block of time.

```jp
今日[きょう]から学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to school from today.*

```jp
何[なん]時[じ]からコーヒーを飲[の]みますか。
```
*From what time will you drink coffee?*

## Rules and exceptions

Word order with particles trips everyone up the first week — that is completely normal. Unlike English, you never put the "from" before the word. A guess like `から家` means nothing in Japanese because the particle must always be attached to the back of the noun.

> Because から marks a starting line, it feels very natural with verbs involving movement (like 行[い]く or 来[く]る) or continuous actions that have a clear beginning.

## Contrast

You already know a few ways to mark locations and times, and it is easy to get them mixed up. Let's look at に and から. 

Think of に as an arrow pointing at your destination. から is the starting block you push off from. Swap them, and the entire direction of your sentence reverses.

```jp
日本[にほん]に行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to Japan.*

```jp
日本[にほん]から来[らい]ました。
```
*I came from Japan.*

The same logic applies to time. The particle に pinpoints an exact moment something happens, while から just tells you when the block of time begins.

```jp
朝[あさ]に本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。
```
*I will read a book in the morning.*

```jp
朝[あさ]から本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。
```
*I will read a book from the morning.*

Now you can pin down exactly where and when things start. Hold onto this starting point — soon we will meet the particle まで (until), which lets you cap the other end of the timeline!
caution_notes: Japanese particles always attach to the end of the noun, so Noun + から translates to 'from Noun', never the other way around.
While に pinpoints an exact destination or time, から only marks the starting point where the action originates.

You're waiting for a friend at a coffee shop. They text you that they're running late, and you want to reply, "I'll wait until noon." You know the words for "noon" and "wait," but you need a way to draw a line in the time.

Enter まで. It acts like a boundary marker, setting the exact point where an action stops.

```jp
昼[ひる]まで待[ま]ちます。
```
*I will wait until noon.*

## Drawing the line

まで attaches directly to the end of a noun. You can think of it as meaning *until* when you're talking about time, or *as far as* when you're talking about physical space.

If you're explaining how far you plan to walk with someone, you just attach it to the location:

```jp
駅[えき]まで歩[ある]きます。
```
*I will walk as far as the station.*

Notice how the rule is exactly the same for both time and place? Japanese loves this kind of consistency. You take the limit (noon, the station), tag it with まで, and follow it up with your verb.

## The dynamic duo: から and まで

You already know that から marks a starting point (*from*). Because から sets the start and まで sets the end, they show up together constantly to express "from X to Y."

```jp
朝[あさ]から晩[ばん]まで遊[あそ]びます。
```
*I will play from morning until evening.*

This combo works perfectly for physical distances, too. You just bracket your start and end points.

```jp
家[いえ]から学[がっ]校[こう]まで歩[ある]きます。
```
*I will walk from the house to school.*

> When using まで with time, the action needs to be something continuous that fills the time up to the limit, like sleeping, playing, or waiting.

## Setting limits: まで against へ

You learned earlier that へ indicates the direction you are heading. So, how is that different from using まで with a place? Let's look at them side by side.

```jp
海[うみ]へ行[い]きます。
```
*I will go toward the sea.*

```jp
海[うみ]まで行[い]きます。
```
*I will go as far as the sea.*

When you use へ, you're just pointing your compass. The sea is your destination, but it's mostly a statement of where you are headed.

When you use まで, you are emphasizing the *extent* of the journey. You're saying, "My trip continues up to the sea, and that is where the travel stops." It highlights the physical distance it takes to get there.

This particle is all about setting clear boundaries. Hold onto this concept of marking a limit—it becomes incredibly handy when we want to ask questions about those limits using `か` later on!
caution_notes: When using まで with time, the action must be continuous, filling the space up to that limit.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place for dinner, and the food is genuinely great. Your friend asks why you're going back for a third helping — and you want to say *because it's delicious*. But hold on: you don't have adjectives like "delicious" yet in your toolkit, so let's pick a reason you *can* say. Your friend asks why you're not drinking the beer, and the honest answer is: *because I'm a student* (and, let's say, too young). That "because" is から.

から is the workhorse "because" of Japanese. You take your reason, say it as a full sentence, and stick から on the end. That's the whole trick — no rearranging, no special verb form. The reason comes first, then から, then (often) the result.

## How it works

The structure is refreshingly flat: **a full clause + から**. Whatever sentence states your reason, you just append から to it.

Because the clause in front is a complete sentence, it can end in a verb, an adjective, a noun + です, whatever — から doesn't care. Here's a noun-predicate reason (someone *is* something):

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]ですから。
```

*Because I'm a student.*

Notice から sitting right after です. That's the polite pattern, sometimes listed as ですから — but it's really just です (the word that works like *is/am/are*) plus から glued on. Nothing new to memorize.

You can put the reason and the result in one breath. Reason first, から, then the consequence:

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいですから、昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]は肉[にく]です。
```

*Because I'm busy today, lunch is meat.*

Here the reason ends in the い-adjective 忙[いそが]しい ("busy"). から attaches straight to it — again, no reshaping the word. The comma after から is just breathing room; it's optional.

You can also flip the order. Say the result, then tack the reason on afterward as its own sentence ending in から:

```jp
昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]は肉[にく]です。忙[いそが]しいですから。
```

*Lunch is meat. Because I'm busy.*

This after-the-fact version is extremely common in speech — you blurt the point, then justify it. Both orders mean the same thing.

## Rules and exceptions

The big thing to internalize: から attaches to a **whole clause**, not to a noun by itself. English lets you say "because of the rain," gluing "because" onto a noun. Japanese から can't do that alone — it needs a real predicate in front. So you say 寒[さむ]いですから ("because it's cold"), not 寒[さむ]さから for "because of the cold."

You have a choice of politeness on the clause before から. Both of these are fine:

```jp
今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]いですから。
今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]いから。
```

*Because it's cold today.* (polite / plain)

The first keeps です for a polite tone; the second is the plain form. Here's the useful rule of thumb: match the clause before から to the formality of the sentence you're in. In a polite conversation, ...ですから feels smoother; among friends, the plain ...から is normal.

> から carries a slightly *subjective*, personal-reason flavor — it's *your* reason, sometimes with a hint of insistence. That's fine in most speech, but be aware that leaning on it hard ("...から！") can sound like you're pushing your excuse. When you want a softer, more neutral "because," Japanese has another tool (see the closing note).

One more trap: don't confuse this reason-から with the から that means "from" (a starting point). Same three sounds, totally different job. The "from" one attaches to nouns (a place, a time); the "because" one attaches to a clause. Context and what's in front of it tell them apart.

## Casual speech

In casual Japanese, you mostly just drop the です and keep the plain clause + から:

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいから。
```

*Because I'm busy today.*

You'll also hear だから standing alone at the start of a reply — literally "because (it) is" — used like "that's why" or, with attitude, "like I said." And a blunt だから何[なに]？ means "so what?" These are set phrases built from the same だ + から; you don't need to produce them yet, just recognize them.

## Contrast

You haven't learned any sibling patterns yet, so there's nothing to swap から against inside your current toolkit — which actually makes this the cleanest possible time to lock in one idea: **から = reason, and it lives at the end of the reason clause.** Reason, then から, then result. Get that shape into your ear now.

The only contrast worth flagging is the internal one from the rules section — reason-から (clause + から) versus from-から (noun + から). Keep them mentally in separate drawers.

Because you have this now, a whole category of sentences opens up: any time you can state a fact, you can turn it into a reason. Lock in the shape — reason clause, then から — because the very next "because" you meet, ので, lives in exactly the same space but sounds softer and more matter-of-fact. When you learn it, you'll define it against today's から.
caution_notes: から attaches to a whole clause with a real predicate, never to a bare noun the way English 'because of' can.
Match the politeness of the clause before から to the sentence around it: ...ですから in polite speech, plain ...から among friends.
Don't confuse reason-から (clause + から) with the から that means 'from' (noun + から); they look identical but attach to different things.

example_sentences.english: Since there's no time, I'll hurry.
example_sentences.furigana: 時[じ]間[かん]がないので、急[いそ]ぎます。
病[びょう]気[き]なので、休[やす]みます。

example_sentences.english: I'll buy it because it's cheap.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at your friend's place and their little sister is asleep on the couch. Someone turns the music up and you want to gently explain *why* everyone should keep it down — not bark an order, just point at the reason. In Japanese, the soft way to lay a reason on the table is ので.

You already have から for "because." ので lives in the same room, but it wears softer shoes. It presents the reason as a plain fact of the situation rather than as your personal push, which makes it perfect for explanations, apologies, and polite requests.

```jp
赤[あか]ちゃんですので、こちらはどうですか。
```

*It's a baby, so how about over here?*

## How it works

The core move is dead simple: take a clause in its **plain form** (the dictionary-style, non-polite form of a verb, adjective, or です), and stick ので on the end. The whole thing means "because [clause]."

With a plain verb, you just attach it directly.

```jp
明日[あした]、病[びょう]院[いん]ので、今日[きょう]は家[いえ]にいます。
```

*Because I have the hospital tomorrow, today I'm staying home.*

With an い-adjective, same deal — the adjective is already plain, so ので slots right on.

```jp
これは安[やす]いので、これにします。
```

*This one's cheap, so I'll go with this one.*

Here's the one spot that trips everyone up the first week — that's normal. With **nouns and な-adjectives**, the plain form of です is だ, but before ので that だ becomes **な**, not だ. So it's `noun + な + ので`, never `noun + だ + ので`.

```jp
彼[かれ]は医[い]者[しゃ]なので、こちらがいいです。
```

*He's a doctor, so this way is better.*

```jp
父[ちち]は今[いま]、病[びょう]気[き]なので、私[わたし]が行[い]きます。
```

*My father is sick right now, so I'll go.*

Notice 病[びょう]気[き] (a noun/な-type word here) takes な before ので. Say it out loud a few times — 医[い]者[しゃ]なので, 病[びょう]気[き]なので — and let the な feel automatic.

## Rules and exceptions

The big constraint: ので points at the reason, and the reason clause comes **first**. You don't lead with the result. The shape is always `[reason]ので、[result]`.

> ので attaches to the **plain** form even when your main sentence is polite. So you get 病[びょう]気[き]なので、行[い]きます — plain before ので, polite です/ます at the very end. Mixing plain-then-polite like this is correct and normal.

Because ので frames things as objective fact, it clashes with strong personal commands and blunt opinions. If you're barking an order or insisting on your own will, ので feels too soft and から fits better. For explanations and polite requests, ので is your friend.

One more: don't drop the な with noun sentences. 学[がく]生[せい]ので is a classic beginner slip; it must be 学[がく]生[せい]なので.

## Casual speech

In fast, casual speech ので often squeezes down to んで. It means exactly the same thing — it just sounds more relaxed and spoken.

```jp
今日[きょう]は病[びょう]気[き]なんで、うちにいます。
```

*I'm sick today, so I'm staying home. (casual)*

You'll hear んで constantly in conversation, especially tacked onto a light apology or excuse. It's not rude, just informal — keep the full ので for writing and polite situations.

## Contrast

Here's the pairing that matters. You know から; both から and ので mean "because." The difference is attitude.

- から pushes: it's *your* reason, and it can carry a bit of "so there." It happily sits under commands and strong opinions.
- ので lays a fact down gently: it's just how the situation is. It softens requests and apologies.

Swap them in a request and you can feel it:

```jp
安[やす]いので、これにします。
```

*It's cheap, so I'll go with this one. (calm, matter-of-fact)*

```jp
安[やす]いから、これにします。
```

*It's cheap, so I'll go with this one. (a touch more "because I say so")*

Same information, different temperature. When you want to sound considerate — to a teacher, a station worker, anyone you're being polite with — reach for ので.

That's the whole trick: ので is から's gentler twin, plain form in front, な glued onto nouns. Hold onto this reason-first shape — it's the same instinct you'll lean on soon when we start ordering events in time with てから ("after doing").
caution_notes: With nouns and な-adjectives, use な before ので (医者なので), never だ — 学生ので is wrong.
The reason clause with ので comes first, and ので attaches to the plain form even when the sentence ends politely.
ので frames the reason as objective fact, so prefer から under strong commands or blunt opinions.
In casual speech ので often contracts to んで with the same meaning.

items.explanation_markdown:
Imagine you are studying at the library. You have a difficult book open in front of you, and nothing is making sense. You spot the teacher sitting at a desk across the room. You want to walk over and ask a question.

You already know the noun for teacher, and you know the verb 聞[き]く, which means to listen or to ask. But if you just throw those two words into the air next to each other, the relationship between them is completely muddy. Are you asking the teacher? Are they asking you? Are you both listening to a strange noise in the library?

In Japanese, verbs often need a clear target. When an action involves another person—especially when you are communicating with them or directing a physical action toward them—you need a way to draw a firm line from yourself to that person. You need a grammatical arrow.

## How it works

To point your action at someone, you attach the particle に directly to the noun of the person receiving the action. The basic structure is incredibly consistent: **Person + に + Verb**.

You can think of this に as a targeting laser. It marks the recipient, or what grammar books usually call the "indirect object". Whenever you are doing something *to* someone—speaking to them, writing to them, or calling them on the phone—に is the little piece of grammatical machinery that connects the person to the action.

```jp
駅[えき]員[いん]に聞[き]く
```
*I will ask the station staff.*

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]に電[でん]話[わ]する
```
*I will call a friend.*

In both of these scenarios, the action is moving away from the speaker and landing squarely on the recipient. You are tossing the conversational ball, and the に tells the listener exactly who is supposed to catch it. It acts beautifully as the English equivalent of "to".

This does not just apply to speaking. It applies to any action where something is being transferred from you to another person. If you read a story, the person on the receiving end takes に.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]に本[ほん]を読[よ]む
```
*I will read a book to the child.*

## Rules and exceptions

The "arrow" intuition works perfectly for communication verbs. However, Japanese verbs do not always line up perfectly with English prepositions. This is where you have to start feeling the shape of the Japanese language itself, rather than just translating word-for-word in your head.

The biggest trap for new learners is the verb 会[あ]う (to meet). In English, the verb "meet" takes a direct object. You just "meet a friend"—there is no "to" or "at" involved. Because of this English habit, it is incredibly tempting for learners to leave the particle out entirely or try to guess a different one.

> In Japanese, you do not just "meet" someone; you direct your meeting *at* them. The verb 会[あ]う essentially demands に to mark the person you are encountering.

```jp
今日[きょう]、彼[かの]女[じょ]に会[あ]う
```
*I will meet my girlfriend today.*

Another sharp edge to watch out for is that に only marks the destination of the action. It does not dictate what is being transferred or where the action is physically taking place. If you are at a hospital and you are asking a doctor a question, the doctor gets the に because they are the target of the question.

## Casual speech

When you listen to native speakers chatting informally, you will notice that particles sometimes get swallowed or dropped entirely to save breath. Topic markers often vanish into thin air.

However, に is a structural load-bearing particle. While other markers frequently disappear in casual Japanese, dropping に when marking a recipient is much rarer. If you drop it, the listener might completely lose track of who is doing what to whom.

You might hear the sound soften or blend very quickly into the surrounding vowels in fast, casual speech, but the grammatical beat is almost always there. When you are speaking casually with a friend, keep your に firmly attached to the recipient.

```jp
お母[はは]さんに電[でん]話[わ]する
```
*I will call mom.*

## Contrast: Directing vs. sharing

You already know the particle と, which connects nouns exhaustively and can mean "with" when doing an action alongside someone. Because English uses "with" and "to" somewhat interchangeably in certain social contexts ("I talked to him" vs. "I talked with him"), it is very easy to mix up に and と.

When you use に, you are emphasizing a one-way transfer. You are the one initiating the action, and the other person is the passive receiver. When you use と, you are emphasizing a shared, two-way action. You and the other person are engaged in it together as equals.

```jp
男[おとこ]の人[ひと]に話[はな]す
```
*I will speak to the man.*

```jp
男[おとこ]の人[ひと]と話[はな]す
```
*I will speak with the man.*

Swapping one for the other completely changes the dynamic of the interaction. Using に feels like you are giving a report, delivering news, or directing information at him. Using と feels like a mutual back-and-forth conversation. Both are grammatically correct, but they paint very different pictures of the room.

## Contrast: Destination vs. origin

You also already know the particle から, which marks a starting point or origin ("from"). Since に marks the destination, these two particles live on opposite ends of the same conceptual road. Using them with the exact same verb highlights exactly how powerful particles are in Japanese.

```jp
父[ちち]から聞[き]く
```
*I will hear it from my father.*

```jp
父[ちち]に聞[き]く
```
*I will ask my father.*

Notice how the verb 聞[き]く radically shifts its English translation depending entirely on the particle. When the arrow points away from your father (から), he is the source, so you are "hearing" information originating from him. When the arrow points toward him (に), he is the destination, so you are "asking" him a question.

## Contrast: Target vs. location

You also know the particle で, which marks the location where an action happens or the tool you use to complete an action. When you are learning to use に, it is important not to confuse the target of your action with the location of your action.

Imagine you are sitting at a coffee shop, and you decide to call your older brother. The coffee shop is the location where the action occurs, so it takes で. Your brother is the target receiving the phone call, so he takes に.

```jp
喫[きっ]茶[さ]店[みせ]でお兄[あに]さんに電[でん]話[わ]する
```
*I will call my older brother at the coffee shop.*

The particles act as strict job titles for the nouns in the sentence. No matter what order you put the words in, the に ensures your older brother is always the one whose phone is ringing. The で ensures the coffee shop is always the place you are sitting while you make the call.

Hold onto this concept of に acting as a one-way targeting laser. You will soon learn sentence-ending tags like よ, which add strong assertion and emphasis to your statements (like saying "I'm telling *you*!"). When you start emphasizing your sentences later, knowing exactly who you are pointing your verbs at will make your Japanese feel incredibly sharp and intentional.
caution_notes: The verb 会う (to meet) requires に to mark the person you are meeting, unlike the English verb which takes a direct object.
The particle に only marks the destination or recipient of an action, not what is being transferred.
Do not drop に in casual speech when marking a recipient, as it can cause the listener to lose track of who is receiving the action.

items.mnemonic_text: か at the end turns a statement into a question.

example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]ですか。
行[い]きますか。
これは何[なに]ですか。
いくらですか。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are sitting at a restaurant with a coworker. They are staring intently at the menu, entirely unable to decide, and you want to ask what they are going to eat. 

In English, turning a simple statement of fact into a question requires you to scramble the entire sentence. "You eat" gets dismantled, flipped around, and rebuilt into "What will you eat?" 

One of the biggest reliefs of Japanese grammar is that you never have to do that. You do not rearrange the sentence structure at all. Instead, you simply pull a single syllable from your grammatical toolkit and snap it onto the very end of the sentence. 

That little syllable is か.

```jp
何[なに]を食[た]べますか。
```
*What will you eat?*

## How it works

Think of か as a spoken question mark. Historically, the Japanese writing system did not use any punctuation at all. There were no commas, no periods, and certainly no question marks. Because everything was written in a continuous, unbroken stream of characters, the language needed a dedicated word to signal that a sentence was an inquiry rather than a fact.

To use it, take a complete, polite statement—ending in either the polite verb suffix ます or the copula です (the word that works like *is/am/are*)—and simply add か to the very end. The particle takes care of all the grammatical heavy lifting.

```jp
明日[あした]、本[ほん]を読[よ]みますか。
```
*Will you read a book tomorrow?*

```jp
あの人[ひと]は学[がく]生[せい]ですか。
```
*Is that person a student?*

One of the best things about this particle is how cleanly it stacks with the rest of the language. When you want to ask a specific question, the question word simply slots into the exact space where the answer would normally live. 

Let's say you want to talk about returning from a location. First, look at a standard statement using the starting-point particle から.

```jp
図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]から帰[かえ]ります。
```
*I will return from the library.*

If you don't know where the person is returning from, you do not move any words to the front of the sentence. You simply swap the location (図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]) for the question word (どこ), leave the particle から exactly where it is, and lock the sentence with か.

```jp
どこから帰[かえ]りますか。
```
*Where will you return from?*

This modular logic works with any particle you already know, like the recipient marker に.

```jp
誰[だれ]に話[はな]しますか。
```
*Who will you speak to?*

## Rules and exceptions

Because this particle explicitly labels the sentence as a question, you generally do not need a written question mark in standard Japanese. A polite sentence ending in か typically finishes with a standard full stop (。).

> You will absolutely see question marks used on the internet, in manga, and in text messages to add visual emotion, but in clean, standard writing, the particle does all the work.

Another detail to watch is your intonation—the rising or falling pitch of your voice at the end of a sentence. In English, we rely heavily on a rising pitch to make a question sound like a question. In Japanese, because か is doing the mechanical work, your intonation does not need to spike aggressively. A slight, gentle rise is natural, but pitching your voice sky-high can sound overly dramatic.

## Casual speech

This is where the textbook rules break down in real life, and it trips up almost everyone in their first week of speaking.

The rule to "just add か" only applies when you are speaking politely, using です or ます. When you drop those polite endings to speak casually with friends, the rules change entirely. In casual speech, you **do not** add か to the end of a plain verb.

If you say `お茶を飲むか` (Will you drink tea?) instead of polite `お茶を飲みますか`, you will sound incredibly rough. It gives off the abrasive vibe of a tough guy in an action movie or someone aggressively grumbling to themselves.

Instead, modern casual Japanese drops the particle completely. You simply state the plain phrase and raise your intonation sharply at the end. Because the particle is gone, this is the one time standard Japanese actually relies on a written question mark to show that tone.

```jp
お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]む？
```
*Will you drink tea?*

## Contrast: The power of one syllable

The power of a single syllable is immense in Japanese. Because the language relies so heavily on context, subjects like "I" and "you" are almost always dropped. 

When you state a fact without a question marker, the listener automatically assumes you are talking about yourself or an established truth. The moment you attach the particle, the focus pivots immediately to the listener. It is a minimal pair where swapping nothing for something changes the entire reality of the conversation.

```jp
今日[きょう]、肉[にく]を食[た]べます。
```
*I will eat meat today.*

```jp
今日[きょう]、肉[にく]を食[た]べますか。
```
*Will you eat meat today?*

Without か, you are declaring your own dinner plans. The moment you add it, you are now asking about theirs.

Hold onto this idea of sentence-ending particles changing the whole mood of a statement—it becomes incredibly important when we meet ね to ask for agreement later on.
caution_notes: In formal writing, a sentence ending in か typically finishes with a standard full stop (。) rather than a question mark.
Never attach か directly to a casual verb; instead, drop the particle entirely and just use a rising intonation.

items.mnemonic_text: ね seeks agreement: '..., right?'

example_sentences.furigana: いい天[てん]気[き]ですね。
暑[あつ]いですね。
おいしいですね。
そうですね。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are sitting in a coffee shop with a friend. You take a sip of your drink, and it is absolutely fantastic. You look across the table and want to share this feeling. If you simply state, "This coffee is delicious," you are just reporting raw data. You are stating a fact into the air. 

But human conversation is rarely just about exchanging data. Most of the time, we talk because we want to connect. You do not just want your friend to know the coffee is good; you want them to take a sip, nod, and agree with you. You want to share the space. 

To build that connection in Japanese, you do not need to change your vocabulary or learn a complex new verb form. You just need to reach for one little syllable and attach it to the very end of your sentence: the particle `ね`.

This single character is the heartbeat of natural Japanese conversation. It softens your statements, invites the listener in, and transforms a rigid textbook sentence into a living, breathing human interaction. When you master it, you stop sounding like a robot and start sounding like a person.

## How it works

The mechanics of this pattern are incredibly forgiving. Because `ね` is a sentence-ending particle (a tiny word that attaches to the very end of a complete thought to add emotional color), it does not force you to change any of the grammar that comes before it. 

Think of it like the caboose at the end of a train. You build your sentence exactly as you normally would, using the polite forms you already know, and then you just hook `ね` onto the back.

If you are ending a sentence with an adjective, it attaches right after the copula `です` (the word that works roughly like *is/am/are*).

```jp
このコーヒーはおいしいですね。
```
*This coffee is delicious, isn't it?*

It works exactly the same way when you are making a statement about the weather, or anything else you are observing together in the moment.

```jp
今日[きょう]の天[てん]気[き]は寒[さむ]いですね。
```
*Today's weather is cold, isn't it?*

It also attaches seamlessly to the end of your verb phrases. If you are looking at a menu and making an observation about a price, the structure remains perfectly intact.

```jp
その本[ほん]は高[たか]いですね。
```
*That book is expensive, isn't it?*

## The power of pitch

While the grammar is simple, the real magic of this pattern lives entirely in your voice. How you change your pitch—your intonation—when you say that final syllable completely changes what you are asking the listener to do. 

When your voice rises at the end of the sentence, tilting up just a bit on the `ね`, you are seeking confirmation. You are essentially asking, "Right?" or "Don't you agree?" You are holding out a conversational baton and waiting for the other person to take it. 

Imagine you are walking down the street with your friend, trying to figure out where you are. You spot a building you recognize, but you want to be sure.

```jp
図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]はあそこですね。
```
*The library is over there, right?*

Because your voice tilts up, your friend knows they need to answer you. But what if the roles are reversed? What if your friend makes a statement, and you want to show that you completely agree?

This is where the falling pitch comes in. If you keep your voice flat, or let it drop slightly on the `ね`, you are no longer asking a question. You are validating what the other person just said. You are nodding with your voice.

If your friend complains about the winter air, you do not need to repeat the whole sentence back to them. You can just catch their baton and agree.

```jp
寒[さむ]いですね。
```
*It really is cold, isn't it.*

This call-and-response rhythm—one person rising to ask for agreement, the other person falling to provide it—is the absolute core of how Japanese people build harmony in everyday life.

## Rules and exceptions

Because this pattern is all about building a shared reality, there is one major edge case that trips everyone up during their first month of speaking. It comes down to a simple rule: you cannot share a space if you are the only one standing in it.

Do not use this particle to ask for agreement on private information that only you could possibly know. 

If you are talking about your own internal feelings, your own name, or your own future actions, the listener has no way to agree with you. If you say `私は学生ですね` (I am a student, aren't I?), you sound like you have bumped your head and forgotten who you are. The listener cannot confirm your own life for you.

> Reserve this pattern for things both you and your listener can observe, experience, or figure out together. If it is entirely in your own head, leave the ending plain.

There is also a physical limit to how much harmony one conversation can take. Because it feels so friendly, new learners often fall into the trap of attaching it to every single sentence they speak. 

If you end five sentences in a row with it, you stop sounding like an empathetic adult and start sounding like a kindergarten teacher talking to toddlers. Use it when you genuinely want to check in with your listener, not just as a nervous verbal tic.

## Casual speech

When you are talking to close friends or family members, you drop the polite armor of `です` and `ます`. When you strip away that politeness, sentences can sometimes feel a bit blunt or sudden. This is exactly where sentence-ending particles do their heaviest lifting.

In casual speech, the particle stays exactly the same, but it attaches directly to the plain forms of your verbs and adjectives. It acts as a cushion, ensuring your statement still feels warm and inviting even without the polite packaging.

```jp
明日[あした]一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]館[かん]に行[い]くね。
```
*We are going to the cinema together tomorrow, right?*

In these very relaxed settings, you can also stretch the sound out into `ねえ`. This elongated version is incredibly common at the very beginning of a sentence. It works beautifully as an attention-grabber, physically drawing the listener's ear toward you before you ask your question. It translates roughly to "Hey..." or "Listen..."

```jp
ねえ、お母[はは]さんはどこですか。
```
*Hey, where is mom?*

## Contrast

You already know how to ask a question using the particle `か`. Since rising intonation on `ね` also asks a kind of question, it is completely normal to wonder how to choose between the two. 

The difference comes down to how much you think you already know. 

When you use `か`, you are standing in the dark. You genuinely do not have the information, and you need the listener to give it to you. You are starting from zero.

```jp
あの人[ひと]は医[い]者[しゃ]ですか。
```
*Is that person a doctor?*

When you use `ね`, you are holding a flashlight. You are pretty sure you already know the answer based on the context, but you are pointing your beam of light at it and asking the listener to look at it with you and confirm. You are starting from ninety percent.

```jp
あの人[ひと]は医[い]者[しゃ]ですね。
```
*That person is a doctor, right?*

Right now, you are practicing how to build consensus and share space with the people around you. But what if you have a piece of information that your listener definitely does not know, and you want to assert it with absolute confidence? Hold onto that thought—it becomes very important when we meet the emphasis tag `よ` later.
caution_notes: Do not use this pattern to ask for agreement on private information that only you could possibly know, like your own name or your own internal feelings.

items.mnemonic_text: よ tells the listener something they don't know: 'you know!'

example_sentences.furigana: これはおいしいよ。
もう遅[おそ]いよ。
危[あぶ]ないよ。

items.explanation_markdown:
Imagine you are at a local diner with a friend. You are both scanning the menu, trying to figure out what to order. Your friend sighs, frustrated because all the meat dishes look pretty expensive, and they are trying to save money.

But you notice something they missed—the fish dish at the very bottom of the page is actually incredibly cheap.

You want to point this out. You want to confidently hand them this new, helpful piece of information so they don't order something they can't afford. In English, you might say, "This one is cheap, you know!" or lean heavily on your tone of voice and say, "Hey, the fish is *cheap*!"

How do you capture that exact feeling of handing over a new fact in Japanese? You don't need to learn a complicated new verb or a formal phrase. You just need one tiny syllable.

In Japanese, to confidently give new information to someone, you use the sentence-final particle よ. It is one of the most common, expressive, and vital tools in the entire language, and mastering it completely transforms how natural you sound in everyday conversation.

## How it works

The particle よ attaches directly to the very end of your completed sentence. 

It is a "sentence-final particle"—a little word that sits at the absolute end of a phrase and tells the listener how to feel about the information. It does not change the grammatical structure of the sentence itself. If you take it away, the sentence still means the exact same thing on paper. 

Instead, it adds a powerful layer of speaker intent. Think of it as a verbal exclamation mark, or a spotlight you are shining on the sentence. It signals to the listener: "I have some information, and I believe you do not have it yet."

```jp
これ、安[やす]いですよ。
```
*This one is cheap, you know.*

In this diner scenario, you saw the price, but your friend didn't. You are handing them that fact.

```jp
私[わたし]は明日[あした]行[い]きますよ。
```
*I am going tomorrow, I'm telling you.*

Here, you are clarifying your own schedule to someone who wasn't sure what your plans were.

In English, when we want to emphasize a point or show that we are telling someone something new, we usually just change our tone of voice. We might say, "I *am* going tomorrow," emphasizing the word "am."

Japanese is a pitch-accent language. Every word has a specific high or low pitch pattern built into its pronunciation. If you try to loudly stress a random syllable in Japanese just to add emotion, you might accidentally change the meaning of the word entirely! Because they cannot just mess with the pitch of the words themselves, Japanese speakers use sentence-final particles like よ to carry all that emotional and communicative weight.

You can attach it right after the polite endings `です` and `ます`. It smoothly wraps up the sentence and delivers it firmly to the listener. Because it flags new information, it is heavily used when teaching someone something, answering a question with a definitive fact, or reminding someone of something they seem to have forgotten.

```jp
今日[きょう]は日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]ですよ。
```
*Today is Sunday, remember?*

If your friend is rushing to get ready for work and they genuinely forgot it's the weekend, this is exactly what you would say. You are correcting their misconception with a solid, undeniable fact.

## Rules and exceptions

Because よ literally communicates "I know this and you don't," it comes with a bit of a sharp edge. It is an incredibly useful tool, but if you overuse it, you can accidentally sound incredibly arrogant.

If you attach it to every single sentence in a conversation, you will start to sound like a bossy know-it-all lecturing the listener. You are essentially saying, "Listen to me, I am telling you this fact. And this fact. And this one."

Use it when you are genuinely sharing a new piece of information, correcting a misunderstanding, or providing a warning. Do not use it for things the listener obviously already knows.

> Be very careful using よ with your boss, your teacher, or anyone of higher status. Because it carries that "let me tell you how it is" energy, using it freely with superiors can easily come across as condescending.

The major exception to the "don't use it with superiors" rule is when you are warning them of immediate danger. In a warning, the new information is urgent and helpful, so the condescending nuance completely disappears.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]、危[あぶ]ないですよ。
```
*Teacher, it's dangerous!*

If a car is rushing down the street and your teacher doesn't see it, you absolutely want to use よ to grab their attention and deliver the warning immediately.

## Casual speech

When you are talking with close friends or family, you drop the polite `です` and `ます` endings. Sentences become shorter and much more direct. 

In these casual conversations, よ becomes even more important for managing the tone of your voice.

A plain, casual sentence can sometimes sound blunt or cold. Attaching よ to the end of a casual verb or adjective adds personality. It shows you are actively engaging with your friend, rather than just stating raw facts into the void.

```jp
私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]忙[いそが]しいよ。
```
*I am busy every day, you know.*

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に食[た]べるよ。
```
*We are eating together, I'm telling you.*

Notice how it attaches directly to the plain adjectives (`忙しい`) and the plain verbs (`食べる`). It flows perfectly in casual speech, keeping the conversation lively and assertive without needing the formal politeness of `です`.

## Contrast: The information gap

You have already learned the particle ね, which also lives at the very end of a sentence. Because both ね and よ occupy the exact same physical space in a sentence, learners constantly mix them up. 

But their functions are complete opposites. The difference entirely depends on who holds the information. This is called the "information gap."

Use ね when you believe both of you have the information, and you expect the listener to agree. It bridges the gap and brings you together. It translates roughly to "...right?" or "...isn't it?"

Use よ when you exclusively hold the information, and you are trying to cross the gap to give it to the listener. It translates roughly to "...you know" or "...I'm telling you."

Let's look at the exact same sentence, changed only by the final particle:

```jp
あの映[えい]画[が]、楽[たの]しいですね。
```
*That movie is fun, isn't it?*

In this situation, you and your friend just walked out of the movie theater together. You both watched it. You are looking for agreement on a shared experience.

```jp
あの映[えい]画[が]、楽[たの]しいですよ。
```
*That movie is fun, I'm telling you.*

In this situation, you watched the movie last week, but your friend has never seen it. They ask you if it's worth watching. You are handing them your review.

If you mix these up, the conversation gets weird fast. If you try to tell a friend about a brand new movie they haven't seen using ね, they will be very confused—how can they agree that it's fun if they have never experienced it? 

If you walk out of a movie you just saw together and use よ, your friend might think you are lecturing them about a movie they literally just watched sitting right next to you.

Always ask yourself: "Do we both know this, or am I teaching them something?"

You are officially ready to start sharing your knowledge, giving recommendations, and correcting misconceptions. Hold onto this feeling of pinpointing exactly what you want to emphasize—it will be incredibly useful when we start setting boundaries and limits with grammar like だけ (only) a little later on in your journey.
caution_notes: Avoid overusing よ with superiors or in every sentence, as the "I know something you don't" nuance can make you sound like a condescending know-it-all.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're describing your morning to a friend, and you want to say two things that happened in a row: you woke up, and then you ate breakfast. In English you'd just drop an "and" between them. In Japanese, you don't reach for a word that means "and" — you bend the first verb into a new shape called the て形[けい] (te-form), and that shape does the connecting for you.

Watch it link two actions into one smooth sentence:

```jp
起[お]きて、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```

*I wake up and eat breakfast.*

The first verb 起[お]きる became 起[お]きて, and that little て is doing all the work of "and then." The second verb stays polite and normal (食[た]べます), carrying the tense for the whole sentence. That's the core idea: the て形[けい] is a connector that hands the tense and politeness off to whatever comes after it.

## How it works

The て形[けい] (the connective form — the shape a verb takes when it needs to hook onto something) is built from the plain dictionary form of the verb. How you build it depends on which group the verb belongs to.

**Ichidan verbs** (the "る-droppers", like 食[た]べる and 見[み]る) are the easy ones. Drop the る, add て. That's it.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて
```

*to eat → eating / eat and…*

So 見[み]る becomes 見[み]て, 起[お]きる becomes 起[お]きて, 寝[ね]る becomes 寝[ね]て. One clean rule, no surprises.

**Godan verbs** are messier, because the ending sound changes depending on the last kana. This is the part everyone has to drill, so here's the whole map:

- く → いて (書[か]く → 書[か]いて)
- ぐ → いで (the voiced version keeps its voicing: で, not て)
- ぶ・む・ぬ → んで (飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで, 遊[あそ]ぶ → 遊[あそ]んで)
- す → して (話[はな]す → 話[はな]して)
- う・つ・る → って (買[か]う → 買[か]って, 待[ま]つ → 待[ま]って, 帰[かえ]る → 帰[かえ]って)

Here's the intuition, not just the chart: the sounds cluster by what's easy to say. The nasal-ish endings (ぶ・む・ぬ) all collapse into んで, and the "small tongue-tap" endings (う・つ・る) all collapse into って. You're not memorizing five random rules — you're memorizing three sound families.

```jp
書[か]いて
飲[の]んで
待[ま]って
```

*writing / drinking / waiting (all te-form)*

**The irregulars** are just two verbs, and you already know both. 来[く]る becomes 来[らい]て, and する becomes して. 行[い]く looks godan but breaks the く→いて rule — it goes to 行[い]って, not `行いて`. That one exception bites everyone, so tuck it away now.

Put it all together and you can chain a whole morning:

```jp
毎[まい]朝[あさ]起[お]きて、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```

*Every morning I get up and eat breakfast.*

Notice again: only the *last* verb is 食[た]べます. Everything before it rides on the て形[けい], and the politeness plus the tense live entirely in that final verb.

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest thing to understand: **the て形[けい] carries no tense and no politeness by itself.** It's a hinge. Whether the sentence is polite or plain, present or past, is decided by the verb at the very end.

That means to talk about the past, you don't touch the て形[けい] at all — you only change the final verb.

```jp
起[お]きて、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べました。
```

*I got up and ate breakfast.*

Same 起[お]きて as before. Only 食[た]べます turned into 食[た]べました, and suddenly the whole thing is in the past. The て form never conjugates for tense — resist the urge to invent a past te-form.

> 行[い]く → 行[い]って is the one you'll get wrong. By the く→いて rule you'd expect `行いて`, but it isn't. It's 行[い]って, patterning with the う・つ・る family instead.

One more constraint: don't use ます-form before the て. Learners fresh off the polite endings sometimes write `食べますて`. That's not a thing. The て attaches to the plain verb stem, never to ます.

## Casual speech

The te-form itself doesn't contract much, but it has one very common everyday job: it becomes a soft command or request on its own. Said with a rising, gentle tone, a bare て形[けい] means "do this, please" in casual speech.

```jp
起[お]きて。
```

*Get up. / Wake up. (casual, spoken to someone close)*

You'd say this to a family member who's oversleeping, not to your boss. It's warm and informal. The fuller polite request form is coming later, but this stripped-down version is what you'll actually hear at home.

## Contrast

You already know ます, ました, and ません — the polite endings that finish a sentence and lock in the tense. The te-form lives in a completely different spot: it never finishes a sentence (except the casual command above), it *connects* to more.

Compare a sentence that stops after one action with one that chains two:

```jp
毎[まい]朝[あさ]、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```

*Every morning I eat breakfast.*

That's complete — ます closes it. Now put an action *before* it, and the earlier verb has to become て形[けい] to make room:

```jp
昨日[きのう]起[お]きて、コーヒーを飲[の]みました。
```

*Yesterday I got up and drank coffee.*

The final verb 飲[の]みました handles "yesterday" and the past tense for both actions. 起[お]きて just links in front of it. Swap the final verb's ending — to 飲[の]みます, 飲[の]みません — and you've changed the whole sentence's tense or polarity without ever retouching 起[お]きて. That's the division of labor: **te-form connects, the final verb decides.**

Hold onto this. Once you meet the plain past た形[かたち] soon, you'll notice the te-form and the ta-form are built from nearly the same sound rules — learn て cleanly now and た comes almost free.

That's the whole pattern: bend the earlier verb to て形[けい], let the last verb carry tense and politeness, and you can string your day together in one breath.
caution_notes: The te-form carries no tense or politeness itself — the final verb in the sentence decides both.
行く is irregular: it becomes 行って, not the expected 行いて.
Never attach て to a ます-form; it hooks onto the plain verb (食べて, not 食べますて).
For godan verbs, group the endings by sound: ぶ・む・ぬ → んで and う・つ・る → って.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are sitting in the doctor's office. The doctor turns to you and needs you to open your mouth so they can check your throat. How do they tell you to do that politely? They use the pattern てください (please do).

When you need someone to perform an action—whether you're ordering at a restaurant, giving directions to a taxi driver, or instructing a student—this is your go-to pattern.

## How it works

To make a polite request, take a verb in its て-form and attach ください. 

The て-form is a special verb shape used for connecting actions. ください is a polite word for "please" or "give me." Put them together, and you turn a plain action into a polite request.

```jp
口[くち]を開[あ]けてください。
```
*Please open your mouth.*

```jp
ここに名[な]前[まえ]を書[か]いてください。
```
*Please write your name here.*

```jp
明日[あした]、うちに来[らい]てください。
```
*Please come to my house tomorrow.*

If the verb's て-form ends in で (like 飲[の]む becoming 飲[の]んで), you simply attach ください to that. The structure works exactly the same way.

```jp
水[みず]を飲[の]んでください。
```
*Please drink water.*

## Rules and exceptions

Because ください translates to "please," a lot of learners assume it is the perfect, universally polite way to ask for anything. But Japanese politeness is tricky.

てください is fundamentally a *direction*. You are telling someone to do something. It is polite in its packaging, but it is still a command. 

It is perfect when you have the social right to direct someone (a doctor to a patient, a customer to a shop staff), when giving instructions, or when encouraging someone to do something beneficial for them (like offering food).

> **Careful:** Do not use てください to ask a boss or a superior for a favor. If you say `見てください` (Please look) to your manager, it comes across as bossy. 

## Casual speech

If ください is the polite wrapper, what happens when you are talking to a close friend or family member? You just chop it off entirely.

In casual speech, the request simply ends on the て or で. 

So, instead of the formal `ここでちょっと待ってください。` (Please wait here a little), you would just say `ここでちょっと待って。` It is short, punchy, and completely natural with people you are close to.

```jp
ここでちょっと待[ま]ってください。
```
*Please wait here a little.*

## Directing vs. Inviting

Let's look at how てください feels next to a pattern you already know: ませんか (won't you?). They both involve asking someone to do an action, but the feeling is very different.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に来[らい]てください。
```
*Please come with me.*

When you use てください, you are giving an instruction. You expect them to follow your lead. 

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に来[らい]ませんか。
```
*Won't you come with me?*

When you use ませんか, you are offering an invitation. You are giving them the option to say yes or no. If you want to hang out with a friend, use ませんか. If you are guiding someone who needs to follow you, use てください.

Getting comfortable with the て-form is a huge milestone. Hold onto it—it becomes incredibly important when we learn how to say you are *allowed* to do something with てもいい very soon.
caution_notes: Even though it translates to 'please', てください is fundamentally a direction or command.
Avoid using てください to ask a boss or superior to do something, as it can sound bossy.

items.explanation_markdown:
You get a message from a friend asking what you are up to. You're in the middle of a meal. If you reply with 食[た]べます, it sounds like you're stating a daily habit or telling them you will eat later. To say "I *am eating* right now," you need the pattern ている.

## How it works
To show that an action is currently in progress, take the **て-form** of a verb (which you already know from making requests like てください) and add いる. In polite speech, this becomes います.

```jp
朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べています。
```
*I am eating breakfast.*

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]っています。
```
*I am waiting for a friend.*

This pattern is the Japanese equivalent of the English "-ing" ending. It frames the verb as an ongoing action.

```jp
今[いま]、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っています。
```
*It is raining right now.*

## Rules and exceptions
For most verbs, the ている pattern means "is currently doing." But for a few specific verbs, it means a lasting state. Think of instantaneous actions, like "getting to know" someone. Once you cross that threshold, you remain in the state of knowing them. Because of this, knowing a person or a fact is almost always expressed with ている.

```jp
彼[かれ]を知[し]っています。
```
*I know him.*

> Watch out for the verb 分[わ]かる (to understand). It already describes a continuous state of mind all on its own, so we normally just use 分[わ]かります. Using `分かっている` usually sounds like an annoyed "I already know that!"

## Casual speech: dropping the "i"
When speaking casually with friends, native speakers naturally take shortcuts. It is incredibly common to drop the い entirely. Instead of saying ている, they just say てる.

```jp
テレビを見[み]てるの？
```
*Are you watching TV?*

*(Notice the explanatory の you learned earlier making an appearance here to ask for context!)*

## Contrast: Habit vs. Happening Now
It is very easy to default to standard dictionary or ます forms for everything you want to say, but they have distinct jobs. A standard verb talks about general truths, routines, or the future. The ている pattern snaps the focus to right now.

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]、お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みます。
```
*I drink tea every day.*

```jp
今[いま]、お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]んでいます。
```
*I am drinking tea right now.*

Hold onto this continuous state pattern—it becomes a crucial building block later when we talk about rules and things you *must not* do (てはいけない).
caution_notes: The verb 分かる (to understand) already describes a state, so it usually remains as 分かります rather than taking ている.
When speaking casually, it is extremely common to drop the い and say てる instead of ている.
