example_sentences.furigana: ここに座[すわ]ってもいいですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 写真を撮ってもいいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 写[しゃ]真[しん]を撮[と]ってもいいです。
帰[かえ]ってもいいですか。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place in Tokyo, and the tea on the table smells amazing. You want a cup, but it's not yours to just grab. In English you'd ask "can I have some?" — in Japanese you reach for てもいい, the pattern that asks *is it okay if I…?*

```jp
このお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]んでもいいですか。
```

*Is it okay if I drink this tea?*

That's the whole job of てもいい: you describe an action, then ask whether doing it is permitted — or, without the question, you *grant* that permission to someone else. It's the polite handshake around "may I" and "you may."

## How it works

The build is simple because you already own the hard part. Take a verb, put it into its て-form (the same form you learned for てください and ている), then bolt on もいい.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて → 食[た]べてもいい
```

*eat → eating(-form) → may eat*

The literal pieces are worth seeing once. も means *even*, and いい means *good*. So 食[た]べてもいい is *even if I eat, it's good* — "even doing this is fine," which is exactly how permission feels. That's your *why*: the も is what makes it *permission* rather than a command.

To make it polite, add です on the end. Both of these are correct; the first is plain, the second is the one you'll say to a stranger or a teacher.

```jp
ここに座[すわ]ってもいい。
ここに座[すわ]ってもいいですか。
```

*I may sit here. / Is it okay if I sit here?*

When you're the one *giving* permission, drop the question and just state it. A parent to a child, a host to a guest:

```jp
テレビを見[み]てもいいですよ。
```

*You may watch TV.*

There's also a more formal, more generous-sounding variant: てもかまいません, literally *even doing it, I don't mind*. Use it when you want to sound extra accommodating — a station attendant, say, telling you it's no trouble.

```jp
ここで待[ま]ってもかまいません。
```

*You may wait here (I don't mind at all).*

## Rules and exceptions

The most common early mistake is dropping the も. Learners hear that permission is "て + いい" and write `食べていい` thinking that's the neutral form. In casual speech that contraction does happen (more on that below), but in careful, polite Japanese the も carries the *permission* meaning — leave it out in a formal setting and it sounds unfinished. When in doubt, keep the も.

> てもいい asks about *your own* action or grants one to someone else. It does **not** work as a general "is X allowed here?" sign-style rule. For that broader "is it forbidden?" feeling you'll want a different pattern (coming very soon).

Another sharp edge: adding か makes it a genuine request for permission, and the answer matters. If you ask 飲[の]んでもいいですか and the host says だめ (no good), you don't drink. Without か, you're not asking — you're telling someone it's fine. Mixing those up can make you sound like you're granting yourself permission out loud, which is a little odd.

One more: because いい is an adjective, some learners try to bend it like `食べてもいかった` for the past. Don't chase that at N5 — stick to the present *may / it's okay* meaning, which covers almost every situation you'll meet.

## Casual speech

Among friends, two things happen. First, the polite です falls away. Second — and this is the big one — the も itself often contracts out, so てもいい becomes ていい in fast speech.

```jp
これ食[た]べてもいい。
これ食[た]べていい。
```

*Can I eat this? (both casual)*

Both are casual and both are fine between friends; the second, with the も gone, is the more relaxed of the two. The tone alone (a rising, questioning tone) does the work that か does in polite speech.

> Keep the も in anything written, formal, or spoken to someone above you. The dropped-も version is friends-and-family territory only.

## Contrast

You've met てください — *please do this* — and it lives right next door, because both attach to the て-form. But they point in opposite directions. てください *asks the other person to act*; てもいい asks whether *you* may act, or tells the other person they *may*.

```jp
窓[まど]を開[あ]けてください。
窓[まど]を開[あ]けてもいいですか。
```

*Please open the window. / Is it okay if I open the window?*

The first hands the job to your listener. The second keeps the action with you and just checks permission. Swap one for the other and you've flipped who's doing the opening — a real change in meaning, not just politeness.

It's also worth setting てもいい beside ませんか, the invitation you learned. ませんか pulls the other person into an activity with you — *won't you…?* — while てもいい is purely about whether an action is allowed.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に行[い]きませんか。
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に行[い]ってもいいですか。
```

*Won't you go together (with me)? / Is it okay if I come along?*

The first is a warm invitation you extend; the second is you asking to be let in. Same activity, completely different social move.

Here's the one-line recap: て-form + もいい asks or grants permission — *may I / you may*. Hold onto the shape, because the moment you can say "you may," the natural next question is "and what may I *not* do?" — that's てはいけない, *must not*, waiting for you just around the corner.
caution_notes: In polite Japanese keep the も — dropping it (食べていい) is casual only and sounds unfinished in formal speech.
Add か to ask for permission; without か you are granting permission, not requesting it.
てもいい asks about your own action or grants one to someone else — it is not a general 'is X allowed here?' rule sign.
てください asks the other person to act; てもいい keeps the action with you or lets the listener act — don't swap them.

items.mnemonic_text: て + はいけない forbids it: 'you must not...'

example_sentences.japanese: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。
example_sentences.english: You must not take photos here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここで写[しゃ]真[しん]を撮[と]ってはいけません。

example_sentences.japanese: お酒を飲んではいけません。
example_sentences.furigana: お酒[さけ]を飲[の]んではいけません。
入[はい]ってはいけません。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing in a quiet library, and your friend pulls out their phone to make a call. Before they even tap the screen, you want to stop them — not with a polite "please don't," but with the flat, no-exceptions "you can't do that here." That's the job of てはいけない.

This is the pattern for rules and prohibitions: the sign on the wall, the thing the teacher says, the line you don't cross. It's the mirror image of something you already know — てもいい, which grants permission. Where てもいい opens a door, てはいけない slams it shut.

```jp
ここで電[でん]話[わ]を使[つか]ってはいけません。
```

*You must not use the phone here.*

## How it works

The build is simple because you already own half of it. Take a verb, put it in its て-form (the same て-form you use for てください and てもいい), and attach はいけない. That's the whole machine.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて → 食[た]べてはいけない
飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで → 飲[の]んではいけない
```

*eat → (te-form) → must not eat*
*drink → (te-form) → must not drink*

The polite version just swaps いけない for いけません. Same meaning, more formal register — the kind of thing you'd see on a posted notice or hear from station staff.

```jp
ここでお酒[さけ]を飲[の]んではいけません。
```

*You must not drink alcohol here.*

Why はいけない? Literally いけない is a word meaning "it won't do" or "it's no good." So the whole thing reads like "doing X won't do." That's a useful intuition: you're not commanding a person directly, you're declaring that a certain *action* is not acceptable. The は in the middle is the topic particle — it's marking "as for doing this thing" — which is exactly why it's pronounced *wa*, not *ha*.

```jp
夜[よる]にコーヒーを飲[の]んではいけない。
```

*You must not drink coffee at night.*

## Rules and exceptions

The て-form does the heavy lifting, so every irregular て-form you've already met carries straight over. 行[い]く becomes 行[い]って (not `行きて`), 話[はな]す becomes 話[はな]して, 待[ま]つ becomes 待[ま]って. If your て-form is right, the prohibition is right.

```jp
その部屋[へや]に入[はい]ってはいけません。
```

*You must not enter that room.*

One thing to watch: because いけない ends like a negative, learners sometimes try to negate it again to say "don't have to." That's a different pattern entirely, and stacking negatives here just produces something broken. Don't reach for `食べてはいけなくない` — it isn't a thing.

> てはいけない is genuinely strong. It's the register of laws, safety signs, and adults laying down rules to children. Saying it to your host at a dinner party — even about something small — lands like scolding. For softening someone's behavior gently, this is the wrong tool.

The subject is usually left unspoken, because a prohibition tends to apply to everyone or to "you." But you can name who's bound by the rule with は or が when you need to be clear about it.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]はお酒[さけ]を飲[の]んではいけません。
```

*Children must not drink alcohol.*

## Casual speech

In real conversation, てはいけない contracts hard. The ては collapses into ちゃ, so 食[た]べてはいけない becomes 食[た]べちゃいけない. This is everywhere in casual speech — friends, family, anyone you'd already be speaking plainly with.

```jp
それを食[た]べちゃいけない。
```

*You can't eat that.*

The で-form verbs (the ones whose て-form is で, like 飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで) shift to じゃ instead: 飲[の]んではいけない → 飲[の]んじゃいけない. Same logic, just following the voicing of the sound before it.

```jp
今[いま]、帰[かえ]っちゃいけない。
```

*You can't go home right now.*

Even the ending often gets trimmed — people drop off after ちゃ and just let the tone or a trailing だめ carry the "no good" meaning. But for now, ちゃいけない is the reliable casual form to lock in.

## Contrast

Line てはいけない up against てもいい, the permission pattern you learned right before it. They share the て-form base and differ only in the tail, but they're opposites — and that's the cleanest way to feel the meaning.

```jp
ここで写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]てはいけません。
```

*You must not look at photos here.*

```jp
ここで写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]てもいいです。
```

*You may look at photos here.*

One tail says "no," the other says "yes." If you can build one, you can build the other — same verb, same て-form, just choose the door.

It's also worth separating this from てください, your request pattern. てください asks someone to *do* something as a favor; てはいけない tells them an action is *off-limits* as a rule. "Please close the door" and "you must not close the door" are not two shades of the same idea — one is a polite ask, the other is a prohibition.

So: て-form plus はいけない is your "off-limits" stamp, softening to ちゃいけない among friends. When you later want to say "please *don't*" as a gentle request rather than a hard rule, you'll meet ないでください — a much softer way to hold someone back, and the natural next step from here.
caution_notes: Build it from the て-form: 行く → 行って → 行ってはいけない, never 行きて.
The は in てはいけない is pronounced wa, not ha, because it's the topic particle.
てはいけない is strong — the register of rules and signs; it lands as scolding in casual polite situations.
In casual speech ては contracts to ちゃ (食べちゃいけない) and で-verbs use じゃ (飲んじゃいけない).

items.mnemonic_text: て + から = only after this action does the next happen.

example_sentences.japanese: ご飯を食べてから、出かけます。
example_sentences.furigana: ご飯[はん]を食[た]べてから、出[で]かけます。

example_sentences.japanese: 宿題をしてから、遊びます。
example_sentences.furigana: 宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしてから、遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 手を洗ってから、食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat after washing my hands.
example_sentences.furigana: 手[て]を洗[あら]ってから、食[た]べます。

items.explanation_markdown:
You just walked through the door. You are starving, but your hands are completely dirty from the train. You want to tell your family you are going to eat *after* you wash your hands.

```jp
手[て]を洗[あら]ってから、ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```
*After washing my hands, I will eat.*

## How it works

You already know the て-form (the versatile form that lets you link verbs and make requests). To say you will do something *after* doing something else, just take the て-form of the first action and attach から.

The action in the てから half of the sentence always happens first. The second half of the sentence is what happens next.

```jp
うちに帰[かえ]ってから、寝[ね]ます。
ご飯[はん]を食[た]べてから、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。
```
*After returning home, I will sleep.*
*After eating a meal, we will watch a movie.*

## Controlling time

Here is a convenient trick: the てから part of your sentence does not have a tense of its own. It just locks the two events into a sequence.

To change the sentence from future to past, you only need to change the very last verb in the sentence.

```jp
本[ほん]を読[よ]んでから、寝[ね]ました。
窓[まど]を閉[し]めてから、出[で]ました。
```
*After reading a book, I slept.*
*After closing the window, I left.*

## The "because" trap

This trips everyone up the first week, so it is completely normal if it feels weird at first. You previously learned that から means "because." So why does it suddenly mean "after"?

It is all about what the particle attaches to. If から follows a plain verb or a polite `ます`, it gives a reason ("because"). But if it attaches *specifically* to a て-form, the meaning transforms into a strict sequence ("after").

Look at how swapping just the verb form completely flips the meaning of the sentence:

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]るから、帰[かえ]ります。
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]てから、帰[かえ]ります。
```
*Because I will watch a movie, I will go home.*
*After watching a movie, I will go home.*

## Casual speech

When speaking casually with friends, the pattern works exactly the same way. You just drop the polite `ます` on the final verb at the very end of the sentence.

```jp
手[て]を洗[あら]ってから、ご飯[はん]を食[た]べる。
```
*After washing my hands, I will eat.*

> You can only use てから with verbs, because nouns do not have a て-form. If you want to say something like "after the movie," you will need a different pattern called 後[あと]で that we will tackle a little later. For now, master your sequences!
caution_notes: The てから phrase has no tense of its own; you only change the final verb to make the sentence past tense.
Attaching から to a dictionary-form or polite verb means 'because', but attaching it to a て-form means 'after'.

example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は行[い]かない。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're relaxing in your friend's living room. It's late, and you have a long day tomorrow. They ask if you want coffee. If you say コーヒーを飲[の]みません, you sound perfectly polite, but maybe a little stiff for a late-night hangout. It sounds almost formal, like you're speaking to a waiter. How do you casually tell them "I won't drink it" without putting up that formal barrier? You need the plain negative: the ない form.

## Bending the verb

When you first learned to speak politely, you used ません to say you don't or won't do something. The ない form takes over that exact same job in casual speech. To make it, we just need to change the tail end of the verb.

Think of Japanese verbs as falling into a couple of main families. For the verbs that simply drop their final る sound when they conjugate (often called ru-verbs, like 食[た]べる and 見[み]る), the rule is effortless. You just chop off that final る and replace it with ない.

```jp
肉[にく]を食[た]べない。
テレビを見[み]ない。
```
*I don't eat meat.*
*I don't watch TV.*

Now, for the other major family of verbs (often called u-verbs), it requires a slight vowel shift. You take the final syllable of the dictionary form, shift its vowel from an "u" sound to an "a" sound, and then attach ない. 

For example, 飲[の]む ends in the syllable *mu*. Shift that to *ma*, and you get 飲[の]ま. Then add ない. 行[い]く ends in *ku*. Shift that to *ka*, and you get 行[い]か.

```jp
コーヒーを飲[の]まない。
今日[きょう]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]かない。
```
*I won't drink coffee.*
*I won't go to school today.*

There is one special catch with this vowel shift. If your verb ends in the pure vowel う, like 買[か]う (to buy) or 会[あ]う (to meet), that final vowel shifts to a わ sound, not an あ sound. So 買[か]う becomes 買[か]わない.

```jp
新[あたら]しい靴[くつ]を買[か]わない。
友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]わない。
```
*I won't buy new shoes.*
*I won't meet my friend.*

Finally, there are always irregulars that like to break the rules. The only one you need to worry about right now is 来[く]る (to come). It completely changes its pronunciation at the beginning of the word, becoming 来[らい]ない (こない).

```jp
彼[かれ]は来[らい]ない。
```
*He will not come.*

## Talking about the past

How do you talk about the past? When you want to say you *didn't* do something, you already know to use ませんでした.

The casual ない form handles the past a bit differently. To make the casual past negative, you take the ない ending, drop the final い, and add かった. So, ない becomes なかった. 

If you want to casually say you didn't play, you conjugate 遊[あそ]ぶ to 遊[あそ]ばない, and then change it to 遊[あそ]ばなかった.

```jp
昨日[きのう]は遊[あそ]ばなかった。
```
*I didn't play yesterday.*

> **Watch out:** Don't try to mix politeness levels in a single verb. A sentence is either entirely polite (using ません) or entirely casual (using ない). Never say `見ませんない` or `飲まないません`. Choose the single level that matches your relationship with the listener.

## Distance and closeness

The difference between ません and ない isn't a change in dictionary meaning—it's a change in social distance.

```jp
私[わたし]は行[い]きません。
僕[ぼく]は行[い]かない。
```
*I will not go. (Polite)*
*I won't go. (Casual)*

The ません ending puts a respectful, safe buffer between you and the listener. It's the default choice for your teachers, station staff (駅[えき]員[いん]), and people you just met. It shows you respect their boundaries.

The ない form deliberately removes that buffer. You use it with close friends, your immediate family like your siblings (兄[きょう]弟[だい]), and when you are just thinking out loud to yourself. In fact, if you insist on using polite forms with your best friend, it can actually sound cold, like you are intentionally pushing them away. Mastering these plain forms is crucial for building real, close relationships in Japanese.

Once you get comfortable using ない and なかった, you'll start to notice they both end in that trailing い sound. Hold onto that thought—because when you formally learn how い-adjectives (like 大[おお]きい and 小[ちい]さい) conjugate later, you'll find they behave exactly the same way. The language is beautifully consistent once you know what to look for.
caution_notes: Never try to mix politeness levels in a single verb—choose either the polite ません or the casual ない, but never combine them.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a party and someone mentions they just got back from Japan. You want to say "Oh, I've been to Japan too!" — not "I'm going," not "I went yesterday," but the bigger thing: *this is part of my life experience.* Japanese has a dedicated shape for exactly that, and it's built from parts you already own.

Here's the move:

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことがあります。
```

*I have been to Japan.*

That last chunk, ことがあります, is the whole trick. Literally it's saying "the fact of having gone exists" — and once you hear it that way, it stops feeling like a weird idiom and starts feeling logical.

## How it works

You take a verb, put it in its plain past form (the た-form, the casual "did" version), and then bolt on ことがある.

The recipe is always the same:

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べた → 食[た]べたことがある
```

*eat → ate → have eaten (before)*

Let's break down that tail. こと is a nominalizer — a little word that turns a whole verb phrase into a *thing* you can talk about. So 食[た]べた ("ate") becomes 食[た]べたこと ("the experience of having eaten"). Then が marks it as the subject, and ある means "exists." Put together: "the experience of having eaten exists." That's your "I have eaten before."

So the two halves you're managing are the た-form on the left and the fixed ことがある on the right. If your た-form is right, you're done.

```jp
私[わたし]はあの映[えい]画[が]を見[み]たことがあります。
```

*I have seen that movie before.*

```jp
彼[かれ]はお酒[さけ]を飲[の]んだことがあります。
```

*He has drunk alcohol before.*

Notice the polite ending lives all the way at the end: あります for polite, ある for plain. The verb in front stays in casual past no matter how polite you're being — that's normal, and it trips people up the first week. The politeness of the whole sentence is decided by that final ある / あります, not by the た-form.

To ask about experience, just add か, same as any polite question:

```jp
日本[にほん]の料[りょう]理[り]を食[た]べたことがありますか。
```

*Have you ever eaten Japanese food?*

## Rules and exceptions

The big one: this pattern is about *life experience*, not about "one specific time in the recent past." If you did something yesterday, you use plain past (食[た]べた), not this. Save ことがある for "at some point in my life, this has happened."

> Don't use たことがある for things you literally just did or do routinely. "I ate breakfast this morning" is 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べました, not 食[た]べたことがあります — the experience frame would sound like you're marveling that breakfast has ever occurred in your life.

To say you *haven't* ever done something, you make the ある negative — turn あります into ありません (or ある into ない in plain speech). The verb in front stays exactly the same.

```jp
私[わたし]はまだこの魚[さかな]を食[た]べたことがありません。
```

*I have never eaten this fish yet.*

A common wrong guess is to negate the verb instead of ある — learners write things like `食べないことがあります`, which means something totally different ("there are times I don't eat"). Keep the verb positive and past; move the negation to the very end.

> The negative goes on ある, never on the front verb. 食[た]べたことがありません = "have never eaten." `食べなかったことがある` is a real but rare and confusing shape — as a beginner, don't reach for it.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, two things happen. First, the polite tail drops to plain: あります becomes ある, ありません becomes ない. Second — and this is the one you'll hear constantly — the が simply gets dropped.

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことがある。
```

*I've been to Japan.*

Drop the が and you get the everyday spoken version:

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことある。
```

*I've been to Japan. (casual)*

Both are fine in casual speech; the が-less one just sounds more like talking than writing. For the negative, ない does the same job: 見[み]たことない means "never seen it." When you're writing or being polite, keep the が and use あります.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know is plain ている — the ongoing-state pattern (Verb-て + いる). It's worth lining these up because both can touch the past, but they point in opposite directions.

ている tells you about a *current* state or an action in progress right now:

```jp
彼[かれ]は今[いま]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べています。
```

*He is eating a meal right now.*

たことがある tells you about a *past experience* that colors the present:

```jp
彼[かれ]はこの料[りょう]理[り]を食[た]べたことがあります。
```

*He has eaten this dish before.*

Swap one for the other and the meaning flips completely: 食[た]べています is "eating now," 食[た]べたことがあります is "has eaten at some point in life." One is a live camera, the other is a résumé line.

It's also worth separating this from the plain past you already use. 見[み]た is "saw (a specific time)"; 見[み]たことがある is "have seen (ever)." If a friend asks どの映[えい]画[が]を見[み]た — "which movie did you watch?" — they mean last night. If they ask あの映[えい]画[が]を見[み]たことがある, they mean "in your whole life, ever?"

Hold onto the こと nominalizer here — that trick of turning a verb into a thing shows up again soon, and the た-form muscle you're building will pay off directly when we meet たり〜たりする for listing actions.

Recap: verb in casual past + ことがある = "have done it before." Negate the ある, not the verb, and drop the が when you're being casual.
caution_notes: Use たことがある for life experience, not for something you just did — 'I ate breakfast this morning' is 食べました, not 食べたことがあります.
Negate the ある (ありません / ない), never the front verb; the verb stays in casual past.
In casual speech the polite tail drops to ある/ない and が is often omitted (行ったことある).

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place and they've been coughing all evening. You want to say, gently, "you should go to the hospital." Not a command, not "you must" — just solid, caring advice. That's exactly the job of ほうがいい.

The pattern means something like *had better* or *should*. You attach it to a verb and you're handing someone a recommendation: this choice is the better one. Here's the hospital line.

```jp
病[びょう]院[いん]に行[い]ったほうがいいですよ。
```

*You should go to the hospital.*

Notice the verb is 行[い]った — the past form — even though nothing has happened yet. That surprises everyone at first. Hold that thought; it's the whole trick of this pattern.

## How it works

There are two shapes, depending on whether you're recommending *doing* something or *not doing* it.

For "you should do X", take the plain past form of the verb (the た-form) and add ほうがいい.

```jp
薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだほうがいいです。
今日[きょう]は休[やす]んだほうがいいですよ。
```

*You should take medicine.*
*You should rest today.*

Why the past form for future advice? Think of ほう as "the ~ side / the ~ option" (it's the same 方[ほう] you'll meet in comparisons). You're literally saying "the *having-taken-medicine* side is good" — you picture the action as already done and judge that outcome as the better one. The past form freezes the action into a completed picture you can weigh.

For "you should *not* do X", use the plain negative — the ない-form — and add ほうがいい. This one stays present, no past trickery.

```jp
そのお酒[さけ]を飲[の]まないほうがいいです。
今日[きょう]は泳[およ]がないほうがいいですよ。
```

*You'd better not drink that alcohol.*
*You'd better not swim today.*

So the split is clean: **positive advice → past (た) + ほうがいい**, **negative advice → ない + ほうがいい**. That asymmetry looks odd but it's fixed and reliable.

You can make the whole thing more polite by keeping です on the end (ほうがいいです), or leave it off for plain speech (ほうがいい). And you can soften it further by tacking よ on the end, which makes it feel like a friendly heads-up rather than a verdict.

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest trap is reaching for the plain *present* form on the positive side. 行[い]くほうがいい isn't the natural advice pattern — for a specific recommendation to a specific person, you want 行[い]ったほうがいい.

> For concrete, in-the-moment advice ("you should go *now*"), use the past form: 行[い]ったほうがいい. The present form 行[い]くほうがいい drifts toward general comparison ("going is the better option, in general") and sounds weaker as personal advice.

The negative side has no such split — it's always ない, never past.

```jp
たくさん食[た]べないほうがいいですよ。
```

*You'd better not eat a lot.*

One more thing about tone: ほうがいい is genuinely stronger than a bare suggestion. When you say 休[やす]んだほうがいい, you're implying there's a real downside to *not* resting. For a lighter "how about resting?" you'd reach for something else entirely (you already know どうですか for that). Save ほうがいい for when you mean it.

## Casual speech

Drop the です and you're already casual: 飲[の]んだほうがいい. In fast speech people often shorten ほう to ほ and swallow the が, so ほうがいい can come out sounding like *ほうがいい* run together — you'll hear it, you don't need to produce it. The safe casual form is simply the plain one with よ:

```jp
早[はや]く寝[ね]たほうがいいよ。
```

*You'd better go to sleep early.*

That よ is doing a lot of work — it turns a flat statement into "hey, just so you know." Very common when you're looking out for a friend.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know is かもしれない, *might / maybe*. They feel related but do opposite jobs. かもしれない reports a possibility; ほうがいい pushes a choice.

```jp
明日[あした]は雨[あめ]かもしれません。
傘[かさ]を持[も]ったほうがいいですよ。
```

*It might rain tomorrow.*
*You'd better take an umbrella.*

See how the first sentence just floats a possibility, and the second one leans in with a recommendation because of it. Swap them and it breaks: you can't advise with かもしれない, and ほうがいい can't merely speculate.

It also brushes up against と思[おも]う, *I think that*. と思[おも]う is your private opinion; ほうがいい is a recommendation aimed at the listener. "この本[ほん]はいいと思[おも]う" says what *you* feel; "この本[ほん]を読[よ]んだほうがいい" tells the other person what to *do*. Same warmth, different direction.

## Closing

Recap: past (た) form for "you should," ない form for "you'd better not," both capped with ほうがいい — and add です or よ to set the tone. The past-tense-for-future-advice quirk is the one to burn in.

Hold onto the ない side of this pattern — that plain negative form is the same building block you'll need soon when we meet まだ〜ていない, "haven't done it yet."
caution_notes: For positive advice use the plain past (た) form: 行ったほうがいい, not 行くほうがいい.
For negative advice always use the plain negative (ない) form — never a past form.
ほうがいい is stronger than a casual suggestion; it implies a real downside to ignoring it, so save it for when you mean it.
Add です for politeness or よ for a friendly heads-up; the bare plain form is casual.
